items.title: Security policy
items.text:
This page tells you how to report a security problem in JAVV, and what occurs after you report it.

JAVV is a tool that manages vulnerabilities. Thus we apply to JAVV the same standard that JAVV helps teams to apply. Thank you for your report.

items.title: Report a vulnerability
items.text:
Do not open a public issue for a security vulnerability.

  1. Open the GitHub form Report a vulnerability (Security tab, then Advisories). The form makes a private thread that only the maintainers can see. When we publish the fix, we can name you in the advisory.
  2. Include as much of this data as you can:
    • The component: the backend API, the ingest endpoint, the frontend, a published scanner image, or a job.
    • The version or the commit that you tested.
    • The steps to show the problem, a proof of concept, or a request that fails.
    • The effect of the problem, and the conditions that it needs. Examples of conditions are a sign-in, a specific capability, or a specific cluster configuration.

items.title: What to expect
items.text:
A small team maintains JAVV. These times are our targets. They are not a service-level agreement.

Stage Target We tell you that we received your report 3 business days or less We do the first assessment and give a severity 7 business days or less We release a fix or a documented workaround for a problem that we accept as a vulnerability As fast as the severity requires
  • While we work on the report, we tell you about our progress.
  • If we decide that the problem is not a vulnerability, we tell you why.
  • When we release the fix, we publish an advisory.
  • Before you make the problem public, give us a reasonable time to release the fix.

items.title: Supported versions
items.text:
• JAVV is before version 1.0 and changes quickly.
  • Security fixes go into main and into the next release.
  • Thus we support only the latest release. See Releases for the current release.

items.title: Scope
items.text:
In scope, all parts that JAVV owns:

  • The FastAPI backend, and specially the ingest endpoint. This endpoint reads scanner output that JAVV cannot trust.
  • Sign-in, sessions, ingest tokens, and the access model that uses capabilities.
  • The queries that JAVV sends to OpenSearch. This includes the isolation of each cluster by cluster_id, and injection into the query DSL.
  • The Vue frontend. This includes all problems that can show the data of a different cluster in a browser.
  • The scanner images that JAVV publishes (ghcr.io/danube-labs/javv-scanner-{trivy,grype}) and the Dockerfiles that make them.
  • The CI and release tools in this repository, where a problem can change a published artifact.

Out of scope:

  • Vulnerabilities in Trivy or Grype. Report them to aquasecurity/trivy or anchore/grype. When a scanner version that JAVV pins has a known problem, open a normal issue that asks for a new version. That issue is in scope.
  • Vulnerabilities in OpenSearch, Kubernetes or other dependencies. The exception is a problem that the configuration of JAVV, or the use of the dependency by JAVV, causes.
  • Problems that need an attacker who already controls a cluster, a host or an administrator account.
  • An installation that its operator configured without security, when the documented defaults of JAVV are safe. Some hardening is the work of the operator. See docs/CONFIGURATION.md for each setting.

items.title: Design decisions to know before you test
items.text:
We made these decisions on purpose. If you can break one of them, tell us.

  • A token protects each push. JAVV does not check a signature. Each scanner pushes with a bearer token for one cluster and one scanner. JAVV keeps only a keyed hash of each token, and it compares hashes in constant time. A token for one cluster cannot push the data of a different cluster.
  • The data inspector can only read. It permits only a fixed list of read requests. It refuses the indices that hold credentials. JAVV writes each query to the audit log. A write through the data inspector is a real finding.
  • The backend isolates each cluster. The query layer adds an explicit cluster_id filter to each read. The frontend does not do this isolation.
  • JAVV never writes to the clusters that it scans. The JAVV backend never connects to these clusters. The scanners in each cluster read only the pods, to find the images that run, and the kube-system namespace.

items.title: javv
items.text:
This chart installs the backend and the frontend of JAVV on Kubernetes.

  • It uses the settings and defaults of the JAVV compose file.
  • It runs one backend, which also runs the background jobs.
  • It runs a frontend Service that browsers and scanners both use.
  • It makes Services only. For https, put your own Ingress, gateway or load balancer in front of the frontend Service.

Other charts:

  • OpenSearch comes from the javv-opensearch chart.
  • The scanners come from the javv-scanner chart, in each cluster that you scan.

Deploying gives the full procedure.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster, and kubectl and Helm that can connect to it.
  • bash and openssl. The commands read each secret at a prompt, or make it in place. Thus no secret goes into your shell history or into the arguments of a process.
  • One namespace for this chart and the javv-opensearch chart.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Install OpenSearch, with the password of admin and the password of javv in Secrets: 
    VERSION=0.9.0
read -rs -p 'OpenSearch admin password: ' pw && echo
printf '%s' "$pw" | kubectl create secret generic javv-opensearch-admin --from-file=password=/dev/stdin
unset pw
kubectl create secret generic javv-opensearch-backend \
  --from-file=password=<(openssl rand -hex 24 | tr -d '\n')
helm install store oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts/javv-opensearch --version "$VERSION" \
  --set opensearch.javv.auth.existingSecret=javv-opensearch-admin \
  --set opensearch.javv.backend.existingSecret=javv-opensearch-backend
  2. Make the two JAVV secrets: 
    read -rs -p 'First JAVV admin password (12 characters or more): ' pw && echo
kubectl create secret generic javv-secrets \
  --from-file=secret-key=<(openssl rand -hex 32 | tr -d '\n') \
  --from-file=bootstrap-admin-password=<(printf '%s' "$pw")
unset pw
  3. Install JAVV. The backend signs in to OpenSearch as javv, with the Secret of javv: 
    VERSION=0.9.0
helm install javv oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts/javv --version "$VERSION" \
  --set secrets.existingSecret=javv-secrets \
  --set opensearch.passwordSecret.name=javv-opensearch-backend
helm test javv
    If OpenSearch has its own certificate, from a Secret or from cert-manager, also add --set opensearch.caSecret.name=<the Secret with its ca.crt>. The backend then verifies the certificate of OpenSearch.

items.title: Where the chart comes from
items.text:
• Each JAVV release publishes this chart at oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts, and signs it (Verify the images and charts).
  • From a checkout, use the folder of the chart in deploy/helm/.

items.title: What the chart runs
items.text:
• The backend: one replica with strategy: Recreate, because a rolling update would run two backends for a short time. It has a ClusterIP Service on port 8000, and three probes. The startup probe gives 300 s to the first start, because the backend creates the indices before it opens its port.
  • The frontend: frontend.replicas pods, and the Service that browsers and scanners use, on port 8080. The frontend sends /api, /auth and /readyz to the backend. It replies 502 when the backend does not reply.
  • Both run as the user of their images, 65532, with a read-only root file system and an emptyDir on /tmp.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
• Each backend setting is under backend.config, by the name that the backend reads. Each one has the comment that the compose file gives it.
  • Each value is the default of the backend, except four values. The chart sets them as compose does (The javv chart). Configuring JAVV describes each setting.
  • The secrets are not settings here. The secret key and the bootstrap password come from secrets. The password and the CA of OpenSearch come from opensearch.
  • values.schema.json makes the install fail for a key with a wrong name. This does not apply in backend.config and frontend.config, which accept each name. Thus the chart passes a setting with a wrong name to the backend, and the backend ignores it.
  • backend/tests/test_compose_settings.py keeps the settings of this chart equal to the code.

items.title: Values
items.text: Key Type Default Description backend.config object every setting at its code default. values.yaml has the list. Each backend setting, at its default, by the name that the backend reads (docs/CONFIGURATION.md, "Backend settings"). Set one with --set backend.config.TZ=Europe/Bucharest, or in your values file. The secrets are not here: see secrets and opensearch. backend.extraEnv list [] More environment variables, in the form of Kubernetes (name, value or valueFrom). backend.image.tag string "0.9.0" The release of this chart. release-please changes it. backend.livenessProbe object {"failureThreshold":3,"httpGet":{"path":"/healthz","port":"http"},"periodSeconds":20} Restarts a backend that does not reply. /healthz does not need OpenSearch. Thus when OpenSearch stops, the app works with less, and Kubernetes does not restart it. backend.readinessProbe object {"failureThreshold":3,"httpGet":{"path":"/readyz","port":"http"},"periodSeconds":10} While OpenSearch is unreachable, /readyz replies 503, and the Service sends no requests to the backend. backend.startupProbe object {"failureThreshold":30,"httpGet":{"path":"/healthz","port":"http"},"periodSeconds":10} Stops the liveness probe while the backend starts. The backend verifies that OpenSearch replies, and creates or updates the indices before it opens its port. 30 tries, 10 s apart: ten JAVV_REQUEST_TIMEOUT periods. frontend.config object {"JAVV_BACKEND_CONNECT_TIMEOUT":"5","JAVV_BACKEND_URL":"","JAVV_LOG_LEVEL":"info"} The settings of the frontend server (docs/CONFIGURATION.md, "Frontend server settings"). frontend.image.tag string "0.9.0" The release of this chart. release-please changes it. frontend.readinessProbe object {"httpGet":{"path":"/","port":"http"},"periodSeconds":10} The frontend serves the app without the backend. Thus it stays ready while the backend is down. It then replies 502 for /api, /auth and /readyz, and the app shows "backend down". frontend.replicas int 1 The frontend holds no state. Thus you can run more than one. frontend.service object {"port":8080,"type":"ClusterIP"} Browsers and scanners both use this Service. The scanners push to /api/v1/ingest/scan through it. You need nothing in front of it. Your own Ingress or gateway can point at it. opensearch.caSecret object {"key":"ca.crt","name":""} A Secret with the CA of the OpenSearch certificate. For javv-opensearch with cert-manager, it is <its release>-javv-opensearch-tls. When you set it, the chart mounts it, sets JAVV_OPENSEARCH_CA_BUNDLE to it and sets JAVV_OPENSEARCH_VERIFY_CERTS to true. When it is empty, the backend does not verify the demo certificates. opensearch.passwordSecret object {"key":"password","name":""} The Secret with the password of javv, the OpenSearch user that JAVV signs in as. Use the Secret of the javv-opensearch chart: opensearch.javv.backend.existingSecret there, or <its release>-javv-opensearch-backend. Never use the admin Secret: the backend needs only javv. podSecurityContext object {"fsGroup":65532,"runAsGroup":65532,"runAsNonRoot":true,"runAsUser":65532,"seccompProfile":{"type":"RuntimeDefault"}} Both containers run as the user of their images, with a read-only root and an emptyDir on /tmp. secrets.bootstrapAdminPassword string "" The password of the first JAVV admin, 12 to 256 characters. A longer password stops the backend at start. The backend uses it one time, when that admin does not exist. secrets.existingSecret string "" A Secret with the keys secret-key and bootstrap-admin-password. Set this value, or the two values below. The chart never makes a secret key: a new key stops each ingest token and each session. secrets.secretKey string "" The secret key of the backend (JAVV_SECRET_KEY). It hashes the ingest tokens and the session ids, and it signs the download links. Use a long random string (openssl rand -hex 32), and keep it. If you change it, each scanner gets 401, and each user must sign in again. Each scanner then needs a new token. The chart puts the key in a Secret.

items.title: javv-opensearch
items.text:
This chart installs OpenSearch for JAVV: one node, with its security plugin on and two users with a password.

  • admin: the superuser of OpenSearch.
  • javv: the user that the JAVV backend signs in as.

The chart wraps the official opensearch chart 3.9.0. It sets the same values as the JAVV compose file.

The Service is javv-opensearch, https on port 9200. JAVV signs in to it as javv, with these settings (Connection to OpenSearch):

  • JAVV_OPENSEARCH_URL=https://javv-opensearch:9200
  • JAVV_OPENSEARCH_USERNAME=javv
  • JAVV_OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD from the Secret of javv

This user has only the javv role: the indices of JAVV, their snapshots and the health of the cluster (An OpenSearch of your own).

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A Kubernetes cluster, and kubectl and Helm that can connect to it.
  • bash and openssl. The commands read the admin password at a prompt, and make the password of javv in place. Thus neither password goes into your shell history or into the arguments of a process.
  • An admin password that OpenSearch accepts:
    • 8 characters or more, with upper case, lower case, a digit and a special character.
    • Not a common password.

items.title: The passwords
items.text:
• Each password comes from a Secret with the key password, or from a value that the chart puts in a Secret.
  • The password of admin comes from opensearch.javv.auth.
  • The password of javv comes from opensearch.javv.backend. Use a long random string.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Make the Secrets and install the chart: 
    VERSION=0.9.0
read -rs -p 'OpenSearch admin password: ' pw && echo
printf '%s' "$pw" | kubectl create secret generic javv-opensearch-admin --from-file=password=/dev/stdin
unset pw
kubectl create secret generic javv-opensearch-backend \
  --from-file=password=<(openssl rand -hex 24 | tr -d '\n')
helm install javv-opensearch oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts/javv-opensearch --version "$VERSION" \
  --set opensearch.javv.auth.existingSecret=javv-opensearch-admin \
  --set opensearch.javv.backend.existingSecret=javv-opensearch-backend
helm test javv-opensearch
  2. Install the javv chart with opensearch.passwordSecret.name=javv-opensearch-backend.

items.title: Where the chart comes from
items.text:
• Each JAVV release publishes this chart at oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts, and signs it (Verify the images and charts).
  • From a checkout, use the folder of the chart in deploy/helm/.

items.title: What helm test verifies
items.text:
• OpenSearch refuses a request without a sign-in.
  • admin and javv are the only users in the user list of OpenSearch.
  • javv holds only the javv role, and the security API refuses it.
  • OpenSearch refuses readall, one of the demo users that OpenSearch would otherwise add.
  • With your own certificate, the certificate of the https endpoint is valid for your CA.

items.title: Certificates
items.text:
Set What the node uses Default nothing The demo certificates of OpenSearch. Their private key is in the public image. Thus each system that can connect to the Service can read the traffic. The demo admin certificate in the image (kirk.pem) also has full access, with no password. Your own opensearch.javv.tls.existingSecret: a Secret with tls.crt, tls.key (PKCS#8) and ca.crt That certificate, for https and for the transport layer of the node. Thus it needs server and client usage. It must name the Service: javv-opensearch and javv-opensearch.<namespace>.svc. The demo setup stays off. cert-manager opensearch.javv.tls.certManager.enabled=true and issuerRef A Certificate that the chart makes for the names of the Service, in <release>-javv-opensearch-tls.
  • With your own certificate, the node reads a new certificate without a restart. The chart mounts the Secret as a folder, and sets plugins.security.ssl.certificates_hot_reload.enabled.
  • The chart never makes a certificate itself.

items.title: Users and roles
items.text:
• The users file of the image holds admin and six demo users whose passwords are their own names. No setting turns them off.
  • An init container puts a new file in its place, with only admin and javv. It hashes each password from its Secret with hash.sh of OpenSearch, which reads the password from the environment.
  • The javv role and its mapping come from the files/ folder of the chart, as in the compose file. The mapping is admin on all_access, and javv on javv. These files replace the demo files of the image.
  • OpenSearch loads these files at its first start. After that, its security index holds them.

items.title: Change a password
items.text:
A new password in the Secret alone changes nothing: OpenSearch keeps the password in its security index.

Prerequisites:

  • The new password.
  • For your own certificates: a client certificate that the CA in your Secret signed, with its subject in opensearch.javv.tls.adminDn, and its PKCS#8 key.

Steps:

  1. Put the new password in its Secret, or in the value of the chart and run helm upgrade.
  2. Restart the node. The init container then writes the users file with the new password: kubectl rollout restart statefulset/javv-opensearch-master. The old password still works.

  3. Load the file into the security index with securityadmin.sh of OpenSearch. This tool signs in with an admin certificate. With the demo certificates, use the certificate of the image: 

    kubectl exec javv-opensearch-master-0 -c opensearch -- \
  plugins/opensearch-security/tools/securityadmin.sh \
  -f config/opensearch-security/internal_users.yml -t internalusers -icl -nhnv \
  -cacert config/root-ca.pem -cert config/kirk.pem -key config/kirk-key.pem
    With your own certificates, copy your client certificate and its key into the pod with kubectl cp. Run the same command with -cacert config/certs/ca.crt -cert <the certificate> -key <its key>. Then delete the two files.

    The command ends with Done with success. From then on, the new password works and the old password does not.

  4. For the password of javv, restart the JAVV backend. It then reads the new password from the same Secret. The name of the Deployment comes from the name of the javv release:

    • Release javv, as in Deploying: kubectl rollout restart deploy/javv-backend.
    • A release name that holds javv: <release>-backend.
    • Each other release name: <release>-javv-backend.

The same securityadmin.sh command loads the role file and the mapping file. Use -f config/opensearch-security/roles.yml -t roles, then -f config/opensearch-security/roles_mapping.yml -t rolesmapping. Do this for an OpenSearch that started without these files, or for a release that changes the role.

items.title: javv-scanner
items.text:
This chart installs the JAVV scanners in one cluster that you scan: a Trivy CronJob and a Grype CronJob.

  • Each scanner pushes its own results to JAVV. JAVV never merges them.
  • Install the chart in each cluster that you scan.
  • JAVV itself, the javv chart, can run in that cluster or at each place that the scanners can reach over HTTP. Connect the scanners gives the full procedure.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text:
• A running JAVV, and an address of JAVV that this cluster can connect to.
  • An admin sign-in to JAVV.
  • kubectl and Helm that can connect to this cluster, and bash.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Find the id of this cluster: 
    kubectl get namespace kube-system -o jsonpath='{.metadata.uid}'
  2. Make one ingest token for each scanner, in JAVV: Settings › Access & tokens › Mint token.
    • For the first token, select New cluster… and enter the cluster id.
    • Select the name of the scanner.
  3. Put each token in its own Secret, and install the chart: 
    VERSION=0.9.0
kubectl create namespace javv-scanner
# asks for each token, so it is not in your shell history or the process list
for s in trivy grype; do
  read -rs -p "$s token: " token && echo
  printf '%s' "$token" | kubectl -n javv-scanner create secret generic "javv-$s-token" \
    --from-file=token=/dev/stdin
done; unset token
helm install scanner oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts/javv-scanner --version "$VERSION" \
  -n javv-scanner \
  --set backendUrl=http://<JAVV's address>:8080 \
  --set trivy.token.existingSecret=javv-trivy-token \
  --set grype.token.existingSecret=javv-grype-token
helm test scanner -n javv-scanner
    helm test verifies that JAVV replies at backendUrl and accepts each token. It does not scan.

Each scanner then runs on its schedule. To start a cycle now, follow the safe sequence in NOTES:

  1. Pause the CronJob.
  2. Wait until no Job of that scanner runs.
  3. Make a Job from the CronJob.
  4. Start the CronJob again.

items.title: Where the chart comes from
items.text:
• Each JAVV release publishes this chart at oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts, and signs it (Verify the images and charts).
  • From a checkout, use the folder of the chart in deploy/helm/.

items.title: What the chart runs
items.text:
• One CronJob for each scanner, with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid. The CronJob never starts a cycle while one of its own cycles runs. It does not count a Job that you make by hand, so use the sequence in NOTES. Kubernetes stops a cycle after activeDeadlineSeconds. The stopped cycle does not run again before the next schedule.
  • A cache of the vulnerability database for each scanner: a ReadWriteOnce PersistentVolumeClaim at /var/cache/javv. Each run first refreshes the database there with the binary of the scanner, from the source of the vendor or from the source in vulnDb. Then it scans with updates off. Thus each image in a cycle gets the same database, and the scan does not connect to the vendor. Trivy uses the misconfiguration rules in its binary.
    • If the refresh fails, the run uses the database in the cache.
    • If the scanner cannot read the database, the refresh deletes it and downloads it one more time.
    • With no database that it can read, the run fails, and its log tells you why.
    • The refresh also verifies the Java database of Trivy. A damaged Java database fails no scan: Trivy only skips the jars that it cannot name.
    • Grype refuses a database older than 5 days.
  • Mirrors: trivy.vulnDb.repository and trivy.vulnDb.javaRepository take OCI repositories. grype.vulnDb.updateUrl takes the address of a list of database builds. Put each other setting that the vendors read in extraEnv, for example GRYPE_DB_CA_CERT or the registry login for a private mirror.
  • Kubernetes access: one ClusterRole. It can list pods, to find the running images. It can get the kube-system namespace, because its UID is the id of the cluster. It cannot read Secrets.
  • Private registries: <scanner>.registryAuth.existingSecret names a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret. Kubernetes puts its .dockerconfigjson key into the scan container as /etc/javv/registry/config.json, and DOCKER_CONFIG points the scanner at it. The refresh does not get the login. With no login, the scanner pulls each image with no sign-in, and it skips an image that it cannot pull.
  • Both scanners run as the user of their images, 65532, with a read-only root file system. They have the cache volume, an emptyDir on /var/lib/javv for the dead-letter file, and an emptyDir on /tmp.

items.title: Images
items.text:
• image.tag is the scanner version from versions.yaml in the repository. JAVV publishes that tag again when it changes the scanner image. Thus the default pullPolicy is Always.
  • To run one exact build, set image.digest.
  • The chart of a release sets the digest. For each scanner, it is the digest that the tag named when JAVV made the release, after cosign verified the signature of scanner-images.yml.
  • A checkout of the repository has the tag only.

Examples: http://javv.javv.svc:8080 in the same cluster, and https://javv.example.com from a different cluster. You must set it. clusterId string "" The id of this cluster in JAVV. When it is empty, the scanners read the UID of the kube-system namespace. When you set it, the scanners verify it: a cycle that reaches a different cluster stops, and does not scan. grype.activeDeadlineSeconds int 19800 Kubernetes stops a cycle that runs for longer than this number of seconds. grype.config object every setting at its code default. values.yaml has the list. Thus each run pulls the image. trivy.registryAuth object {"existingSecret":""} A registry login for the images from private registries: the name of a kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret in the namespace of the chart. When it is empty, Trivy uses mirror.gcr.io/aquasec/trivy-db:2, then ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy-db:2. trivy.vulnDb.size string "10Gi" The cache volume. items.title: JAVV operator docs
items.text:
JAVV finds the container images that run in your Kubernetes clusters. It scans each image with Trivy and with Grype, and it keeps the results of each scanner apart. For each vulnerability, JAVV records each triage decision in an audit log.

These pages are for the people who install and operate JAVV. To learn how to triage findings in JAVV, read Use JAVV. It has a short video for each task.

items.title: Start here
items.text:
To do this Read Install JAVV with docker compose or with Helm Deploying Run the scanners in the clusters that you scan Deploying: connect the scanners and the scanner chart Find the scanner and OpenSearch versions that a release supports Supported versions Change a setting Configuration Calculate the OpenSearch size for your clusters Sizing OpenSearch Learn which parts scale, and what occurs when a part fails Scaling and failures Learn which indices JAVV uses, how long it keeps the data, and what a snapshot holds Indices and data Upgrade JAVV, or go back to the previous release Upgrading and the release notes Verify the published images and charts Deploying: verify the images and charts Send requests to JAVV from a script, or push results from your own tools API and Push from your own script Report a security problem Security

Each JAVV release has its own version of these docs. Select the version in the version menu.

items.title: JAVV API
items.text:
This page describes the HTTP API of JAVV. It is for people who write scripts for JAVV or monitor it. The tasks come first. Then the reference tables give each endpoint, error and metric.

The backend also publishes a description of its API, with each parameter and its limits. It is at /docs and /openapi.json on the backend port, 8000. The frontend does not send these two paths to the backend.

To push scan results from your own tools, read Push from your own script. To connect the JAVV scanners, read Connect the scanners.

items.title: Sign in from a script
items.text:
A script uses the same address as a browser. The frontend sends /api, /auth and /readyz to the backend.

Prerequisites:

  • bash, curl and jq.
  • A JAVV username and password.

Steps:

  1. Set the address of JAVV: 
    JAVV=https://javv.example.com
  2. Sign in. The command keeps the session cookie in the file jar: 
    read -rs -p 'Password: ' pw && echo
jq -n --arg u admin --arg p "$pw" '{username: $u, password: $p}' \
  | curl -sf -c jar -b jar -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data @- "$JAVV/auth/login"
    The reply shows must_change. If it is true, do step 3. If it is false, go to step 4.
  3. Change the password. The new password must have 12 characters or more: 
    read -rs -p 'New password: ' new && echo
jq -n --arg c "$pw" --arg n "$new" '{current_password: $c, new_password: $n}' \
  | curl -sf -c jar -b jar -H 'Content-Type: application/json' --data @- "$JAVV/auth/password"
unset new
    JAVV signs the user out of each session, then writes a new session cookie to jar.
  4. Delete the password from the shell: 
    unset pw
  5. Send your requests with the cookie. For example, show your user and permissions: 
    curl -sf -b jar "$JAVV/auth/me"
  6. At the end of the script, sign out. JAVV then ends the session: 
    curl -sf -b jar -X POST "$JAVV/auth/logout"

Keep the file jar private. Until the session ends, the cookie in it gives access as your user.

items.title: Read a list page by page
items.text:
A list endpoint gives one page of rows. List responses shows the three forms of a list. This procedure reads all the findings of one cluster with the cursor.

Prerequisites:

  • A session cookie in the file jar (Sign in from a script).

Steps:

  1. Find the id of the cluster: 
    curl -sf -b jar "$JAVV/api/v1/clusters" | jq -r '.clusters[] | "\(.cluster_id) \(.cluster_name)"'
  2. Set the id: 
    cluster=<cluster_id>
  3. Read each page, 500 rows at a time. Send next_cursor back as cursor until it is null: 
    cursor=
while :; do
  page=$(curl -sfG -b jar "$JAVV/api/v1/findings" --data-urlencode "cluster_id=$cluster" \
    --data-urlencode size=500 ${cursor:+--data-urlencode "cursor=$cursor"}) || break
  jq -c '.data[] | {cve_id, scanner, severity, state}' <<<"$page"
  cursor=$(jq -r '.next_cursor // empty' <<<"$page")
  [ -n "$cursor" ] || break
done > findings.jsonl
  4. Compare the number of lines in findings.jsonl with total.value of a page. If they are not equal, a page failed. Read the list again.

A cursor stays valid for a short time only. If a page answers 410, start again at step 3.

To stop before the last page, close the cursor. Until then, it keeps one of your open-cursor slots (Exports and reports): 

jq -n --arg c "$cursor" '{cursor: $c}' |
  curl -sf -b jar -X POST "$JAVV/api/v1/cursors/close" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @-

items.title: Scrape the metrics
items.text:
The backend gives its metrics at /metrics, in the Prometheus format.

  • This path needs no sign-in.
  • The frontend does not send it to the backend.
  • Metrics lists each metric.

Prerequisites:

  • A Prometheus that can connect to the backend port, 8000.

Steps:

  1. Let your Prometheus connect to the backend port, 8000:
    • with docker compose: publish the port. Use the ports block in comments under backend in compose.yaml (Ports and access).
    • with Helm: use the backend Service. For a release with the name javv, it is javv-backend.
  2. Add a scrape of http://<backend>:8000/metrics to your Prometheus.
  3. Look at the metrics from a machine that can connect to the port: 
    curl -sf http://<backend>:8000/metrics | grep '^# TYPE javv_'

JAVV gives no alert rules. Make alerts from the metrics that apply to your setup.

items.title: Authentication
items.text:
Each endpoint uses one of three kinds of authentication.

Kind What the request sends Endpoints None Nothing /healthz, /readyz and /metrics. Control the access to these with your network. Also POST /auth/login and POST /auth/logout. Scanner token Authorization: Bearer <token>. Each token is for one cluster and one scanner. JAVV keeps only a hash of the token. The scanner endpoints: ingest, scan scope, scan runs and inventory runs. A token can send data only for its own cluster and scanner. Session The javv_session cookie from POST /auth/login All other endpoints

The session cookie has the HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax flags. It also has the Secure flag, unless JAVV_SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is false (http or https).

  • Session time: a session ends JAVV_SESSION_TTL_HOURS after the sign-in (default 24), or at sign-out. The server decides, not the cookie.
  • Failed sign-ins: after JAVV_LOGIN_MAX_ATTEMPTS failures (default 5) for one username in JAVV_LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MINUTES (default 15), the sign-in answers 429. All cases of a name are one count: Alice and alice count together. A successful sign-in sets the count to zero.
  • One answer for each failure: a wrong username, a wrong password, a disabled user and an expired session all get the same 401. Thus the answer does not show if a username exists.
  • The login body: POST /auth/login accepts only Content-Type: application/json. A body that is not JSON gets 422. A different JSON type, for example application/merge-patch+json, gets 415.

items.title: A temporary password
items.text:
The first admin, a new user and a user after a password reset have a temporary password. The user must change it (Sign in from a script, step 3). Until then, the session can use only /auth/*: show the user, change the password, and sign out. Each other session endpoint answers a well-formed request with 403 password change required, reads included. A body that is not valid JSON gets 422 first.

Each refusal logs a password change required warning with the username. It also increments javv_auth_failures_total{reason="must_change"}.

items.title: A password change
items.text:
POST /auth/password changes the password of the user of the session.

  • The new password has 12 to 256 characters. Each character counts as one, also a character outside ASCII.
  • 401: the current password is wrong, or the session ended. The two get the same answer.
  • 403: an identity provider manages the password of the user.
  • 422: the new password has fewer than 12 or more than 256 characters, or the body is not valid.
  • The audit row comes first. JAVV writes a pwd_change row to the audit log before it changes the password. If JAVV cannot write the row, the password does not change, and the answer is an error.
  • 200 with no cookie: the password changed, but JAVV could not make the new session. Each old session ended, so sign in again with the new password. JAVV logs a password changed, no new session warning and increments javv_auth_failures_total{reason="session_not_minted"}.

items.title: Roles and permissions
items.text:
Some endpoints need a permission. The tables in Endpoints name it. A user gets the permissions of its role. The web app uses the capabilities from GET /auth/me to show or hide its controls. The backend checks the permission again on each request.

At its first start, JAVV creates four roles:

Role Permissions viewer None. The user can read data only. triager can_triage, can_export, can_edit_dashboards security_lead can_triage, can_accept_audit_final, can_export, can_edit_dashboards admin All the permissions, also the permissions of later releases Permission What it allows can_triage Triage findings. Make, change and revoke not_affected decisions. can_accept_audit_final Accept a risk, in a decision or in triage. Make, change and revoke risk_accepted and ignore_rule decisions. Change the state of a risk-accepted finding, also in a bulk triage. Read and export the approvals queue. can_export Download the export files: the findings CSV and VEX, the audit log CSV, the contributors CSV and the approvals CSV. Make an export report and download it. can_edit_dashboards Make dashboards. Change, share and delete your own dashboards. can_manage_tokens Make, revoke and rotate scanner tokens can_manage_users Make users. Change their role, their status and their password. Read the account events in the audit log. can_manage_settings Change the SLA, staleness, retirement and scan scope settings, and the cluster names. Retire a cluster, and bring it back. Read the OpenSearch facts. Start the staleness sweep. Change or delete the saved views of other users. See, change and delete the dashboards of other users, with can_edit_dashboards. Read the dashboard rows in the audit log. can_manage_retention Read and change the data settings: retention, rollover, export lifetime and findings cleanup. Read and take snapshots. Delete a retired cluster. can_restore_snapshot Restore a snapshot can_inspect_store Use the data inspector. Read the status of the background jobs. can_rebuild_state Start the job that builds the current state again can_drop_index Start the lifecycle sweep, which deletes old indices

The Roles card in the web app shows a name and a short text for each permission. It gets them from GET /api/v1/admin/roles. The backend keeps one list of the permissions, in this order.

can_export controls the export files, not the reads. A user without it can still read each finding through GET /api/v1/findings, 500 rows a page.

Each read and export applies the cluster that the request names. Each user can read each cluster. A cluster_id has 8 to 64 lowercase letters, digits or hyphens, and does not start with a hyphen.

items.title: Errors
items.text:
Each answer that is not a success has the same body, with the type application/problem+json:

{"type": "about:blank", "title": "invalid credentials", "status": 401, "detail": null, "request_id": "b169be4a30444fdc"}
  • type: about:blank, or one of these. Match on type, not on title: the title can change.
    • store-read-only on a 503 for a write that OpenSearch refused because its disk is full.
    • cluster-delete-unfinished on a 409 for a cluster whose delete did not finish: a bring back (POST /api/v1/clusters/{cluster_id}/unretire) or a new token (POST /api/v1/admin/tokens). Delete the cluster again to finish it.
    • expiry-passed on a 422 for a decision whose expiry is not after today in UTC, or not after now (POST /api/v1/decisions, PATCH /api/v1/decisions/{decision_id}).
  • title: a short text that names the error.
  • detail: on a 422 from a field check, the list of the fields that are not valid, with the reason for each. It does not hold the value that you sent. Else it is null.
  • request_id: the id of the request in the backend log. The X-Request-ID header of the answer also has it, on each answer. To set the id yourself, send X-Request-ID with 1 to 64 letters, digits or hyphens. If you send no id, or an id that is not valid, the backend makes one.
Status Meaning 400 The ingest body is not valid gzip or JSON. On the other endpoints, a body that is not valid JSON gets 422. 401 The request has no valid session or token. 403 The user does not have the permission, or must change the password first. A scanner token sent data for a different cluster or scanner. 404 The item does not exist. For an item of a different user, the answer is also 404. 409 A different request changed the item first, or the item is not in the necessary state. 410 The cursor or the export expired. Do the request again from the start. 413 The request asks for too many rows, or its body is too large. Make the request smaller. 415 The sign-in body has a JSON type that is not application/json, or a dashboard import body is not application/x-ndjson. 422 A field is not valid. detail names the field. 501 The CSV or VEX export of findings got a past as_of. Make a report with as_of_t instead (A past time: as_of). 429 Too many requests. Some answers have a Retry-After header with the seconds to wait. The title "The search backend is busy" tells that OpenSearch itself has too much work (a full queue or a circuit breaker). That answer has Retry-After: 5. 503 OpenSearch is not available. Do the request again later. The type store-read-only, with the title The store is read-only: its disk is full, tells that the disk of OpenSearch is past its flood-stage watermark. Reads work. Each change that OpenSearch refuses, also a sign-in, gets this 503 until OpenSearch has free disk space. An ingest push gets the ingest 503 instead (Ingest a scan).

items.title: List responses
items.text:
A list has one of three forms. The form comes from how the endpoint pages its rows.

Paging Form Endpoints Cursor {"data": [...], "next_cursor": "...", "total": {"value": N, "relation": "eq"}} /findings, /audit, /scanners/ingest-failures Offset: size and offset {"<name>": [...], "total": N} /decisions (decisions), /decisions/approvals (approvals), /admin/users (users), /admin/tokens (tokens) None {"<name>": [...]} /contributors (leaderboard), /images (images), /images/timeline (events), /findings/top-components (components), /clusters (clusters), /views (views), /dashboards (dashboards), /dashboards/roles (roles), /notifications (items), /admin/jobs (jobs), /admin/roles (roles), /admin/snapshots (snapshots), /scanners/provenance (scanners), /scanners/freshness (scanners)
  • /findings/groups uses a cursor, but it has no total.
  • /notifications puts its rows in items, not in a key with the name of the resource.
  • Some answers have more keys next to the list. For example, /images also has inventory.
  • In a cursor list, total is an object. In an offset list, total is a number.

Read a key by its name, and check that it exists. In jq, a key that does not exist gives null, and the length of null is 0. That looks the same as an empty list.

items.title: Endpoints
items.text:
In the tables, the Access column gives the authentication, or the permission that the endpoint needs:

  • none: no authentication.
  • token: a scanner token.
  • session: any signed-in user.
  • a permission name: a signed-in user with that permission (Roles and permissions).

The audit log keeps each sign-in and sign-out, and each change to triage, decisions, settings, the scan scope, users, tokens, saved views, dashboards, clusters, snapshots and jobs. It also keeps each query of the data inspector.

Each signed-in user reads the audit log. Only a user with can_manage_users reads the account events: the rows with entity_type user (sign-ins and sign-outs, password, user and role changes) and token (the scanner tokens). For the other users, the three audit endpoints leave these rows out of the list, the counts and the CSV.

Only a user with can_manage_settings reads the rows with entity_type dashboard. A dashboard row holds the whole dashboard, also a private one, and these users can see each dashboard. For the other users, the three audit endpoints leave these rows out in the same way.

items.title: System
items.text:
Method Path Access What it does GET /healthz none Liveness. It answers 200 while the process runs. It does not use OpenSearch. GET /readyz none Readiness. It answers 200 {"status": "ready"} when OpenSearch answers, else 503 {"status": "degraded"}. OpenSearch can answer but refuse writes (its disk is past the flood-stage watermark), or be red (part of its data is not available). Then the answer is 200 with "checks": {"store": "read-only"} or "red". Reads still work, so the backend stays in service. GET /metrics none The metrics, in the Prometheus format (Metrics) GET /api/v1/meta session The versions that the backend runs: version (the JAVV release), mapping_version, envelope_versions (the ingest schema versions that it accepts), opensearch_version and python_version. If OpenSearch does not answer, opensearch_version is null.

The backend also writes the release and the mapping version in its bootstrap complete log line.

items.title: Scanner endpoints
items.text:
The scanners use these endpoints. Each one applies to the cluster and the scanner of the token, never to values in the body. Push from your own script gives the order of the calls in a scan cycle.

Method Path Access What it does POST /api/v1/ingest/scan token Accepts the results of one scan (Ingest a scan) GET /api/v1/scan-scope token Gives the scan scope of the cluster of the token POST /api/v1/scan-runs token Gives the next scan_order for the cluster and scanner of the token. Each value is larger than the one before. POST /api/v1/inventory-runs token Closes the inventory of a scan cycle. Body: {scan_run_id, expected_count, started_at}. The backend counts the images that it received. The run is committed only if that count is complete. A repeated call gives the first result again.

items.title: Sign-in and sessions
items.text: Method Path Access What it does POST /auth/login none Signs in and sets the session cookie. The username can be in any case: the backend looks for the name as typed, then for the name in lower case. A wrong username or password gets 401. Too many failures get 429 (Authentication). POST /auth/logout none Signs out. It ends the session of the cookie on the server, if the request has a cookie, and deletes the cookie. The answer is 204, also with no session. POST /auth/password session Changes your password. Body: {current_password, new_password}. It signs you out of each session and sets a new cookie. The rules and the refusals are in A password change. GET /auth/me session Your user: username, role, capabilities and must_change

items.title: Admin
items.text: Method Path Access What it does GET/POST /api/v1/admin/tokens can_manage_tokens GET lists the scanner tokens, newest first, with size (1 to 1000, default 100), offset (0 to 9000) and an optional cluster_id. POST makes a token for {cluster_id, scanner, expiry}. The answer shows the token one time only. A cluster with a delete that did not finish gets 409. A token for a deleted cluster's ID onboards that cluster again: JAVV then keeps its new data. POST /api/v1/admin/tokens/{token_id}/revoke can_manage_tokens Disables a token POST /api/v1/admin/tokens/{token_id}/rotate can_manage_tokens Makes a new token, with a new id, for the same cluster, scanner and expiry. Then it disables the old token. A revoked token and an expired token get 409, and nothing changes. Make a new token for them. GET/POST /api/v1/admin/users can_manage_users GET lists the users, with size (1 to 1000, default 100) and offset (0 to 9000). POST makes a user with {username, temp_password, role}. A username has 3 to 64 lower-case letters, digits, dots, underscores or hyphens. A username with a capital letter gets 422, and so do system and fleet. A username that exists gets 409. PATCH /api/v1/admin/users/{username}/role can_manage_users Changes the role of a user, and signs that user out of each session PATCH /api/v1/admin/users/{username}/disabled can_manage_users Disables or enables a user. A disabled user loses each session. The last enabled admin gets 409. POST /api/v1/admin/users/{username}/password-reset can_manage_users Sets a temporary password, which the user must change. It signs that user out of each session. GET /api/v1/admin/roles can_manage_users The roles and their permissions in roles. Also permissions: each permission with its id, a name and a description of what it allows, in the order of the table in Roles and permissions. GET /api/v1/admin/snapshots can_manage_retention The snapshots in the configured repository, newest first. With no repository, configured is false. POST /api/v1/admin/snapshots can_manage_retention Starts a snapshot of findings, javv-images-* and system-* except system-sessions, and answers 202 at once. The scan history is not in the snapshot (Snapshots). With no repository, it answers 409. POST /api/v1/admin/snapshots/{snapshot_name}/restore can_restore_snapshot Restores a snapshot into copies with the prefix restored-. It never writes to the live indices. To use a copy, move it in by hand. GET /api/v1/admin/opensearch-runtime can_manage_settings Facts about OpenSearch: version, health, nodes, roles, heap, discovery.type, path.repo and the security plugin. It gives only these fields. POST /api/v1/admin/opensearch/inspect can_inspect_store The data inspector. The data inspector gives its rules. GET /api/v1/admin/jobs can_inspect_store The status of each of the eight background jobs, and of the scheduler (The jobs list) POST /api/v1/admin/jobs/{kind}/run the permission of the job Starts a job, and answers 202 {attempt_id} (Start a background job)

items.title: The data inspector
items.text:
POST /api/v1/admin/opensearch/inspect takes {method, path, body} and sends only allowed reads to OpenSearch:

  • GET or POST on <index>/_search and <index>/_count
  • GET on <index>/_mapping
  • GET on _cat/indices, _cat/shards, _cluster/health and _nodes/stats. The _cat reads show only the indices of JAVV.

These requests get 422, with the reason:

  • a request on system-users, system-sessions or system-tokens
  • a body with script, script_fields, runtime_mappings, pit or scroll
  • a size larger than JAVV_INSPECT_MAX_HITS.

An answer larger than JAVV_INSPECT_MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES gets 413. A good answer is {took_ms, bytes, cap_bytes, body}. The audit log keeps each query, with the user, the method and path, and a hash of the query.

items.title: The jobs list
items.text:
GET /api/v1/admin/jobs gives {jobs, scheduler}. jobs has one entry for each job kind:

  • the last run: status, requested_by, started_at, finished_at, result and error. A job that never ran has status: idle.
  • stale: true when a run is running, but it stopped its heartbeat.
  • runnable and capability: if you can start the job with POST .../run, and the permission for it. capability is null for a job that you cannot start.
  • schedule: the cron expression from JAVV_JOB_<KIND>_CRON, or null.
  • next_run_at: the next run, in UTC. It is null when the job or the scheduler is off.
  • health, one of these values. The first value that applies is the result:
    1. failed: the last run failed.
    2. off: the job has no schedule, or the scheduler is off.
    3. never_ran: the job has a schedule, but no run.
    4. overdue: two scheduled times passed after the last start.
    5. ok: all other cases.

scheduler is {enabled, timezone}: if this backend runs the schedules, and the time zone of the cron expressions.

items.title: Start a background job
items.text:
POST /api/v1/admin/jobs/{kind}/run starts one of three jobs:

Kind Permission rebuild_state can_rebuild_state staleness_sweep can_manage_settings lifecycle_sweep can_drop_index
  • The other five kinds, and a kind that does not exist, get 404.
  • If a run of the job is in progress, the request gets 409. The scheduler applies the same rule. Thus one run of a kind at a time occurs.
  • ?dry_run=true applies to lifecycle_sweep only. It answers 200 {dry_run, result: {rolled, dropped, errors}} with the counts that a run would give. It changes nothing. On the other kinds, dry_run gets 422.

items.title: Findings: read
items.text:
These endpoints need a session only. Each one needs cluster_id, except POST /api/v1/cursors/close.

Method Path Access What it does GET /api/v1/findings session One page of findings, with a cursor (Read a list page by page). size is 1 to 500, default 50. sort is severity_rank, first_seen_at, last_scan_at, cvss or epss. The last page closes the search of the cursor. With keep_open=true, a page read with a cursor keeps it open after the last page, so you can read an earlier page again. Then close it with POST /api/v1/cursors/close. GET /api/v1/findings/facets session The count of findings for each value of a field, for each scanner. fields is one or more of severity, state, scanner, fixable, kev, disagree, present, ptype, namespaces, assignee, overdue and unassigned. For namespaces and assignee, it gives the 32 largest values. The namespaces, ptype and assignee facets count without the filter of their own field. Thus a value that you pick does not take the other values out of the list. The unassigned facet counts without the assignee values, and it keeps exclude_assignee. On the Findings screen, a click on Unassigned clears those values, so the count is the result of the click. All other facets count with all filters. GET /api/v1/findings/groups session Findings in groups, page by page with a cursor. by is image_repo, image_digest, namespaces, cve_id, assignee, app or ptype. GET /api/v1/findings/top-components session The packages with the most findings, and the count of different CVEs for each scanner. A past as_of gets 422. GET /api/v1/trends/scans · /api/v1/trends/findings session Counts for each day over days (1 to 365, default 30), for each scanner. Trends gives the details. GET /api/v1/trends/ingest-failures session The pushes that the ingest refused after the token check, for each time interval and scanner (Trends) GET /api/v1/contributors session The triage work of each user over days (1 to 365, default 30): actions, time to fix and SLA results. totals gives the same values for the team. GET /api/v1/contributors/export.csv can_export The data of /contributors as CSV. It has one action_<name> column for each triage action. A file larger than JAVV_EXPORT_MAX_ROWS rows gets 413. GET /api/v1/scanners/freshness session For each scanner of the cluster: last_ingest_at and silent_for_seconds. With no push yet, both are null. GET /api/v1/scanners/ingest-failures session The pushes that the ingest refused after the token check, newest first. scanner is necessary. days is 1 to 365 (default 30), and size is 1 to 100 (default 25). Failed pushes gives the fields. GET /api/v1/scanners/provenance session For each scanner: the versions and effective_config of the last committed run, and the last runs runs (1 to 50, default 10) GET /api/v1/audit session The audit log, page by page with a cursor. Filters: entity_type, action, actor and finding_key, each with an exclude_ form except finding_key. entity_type, action and actor take several values, for example actor=a&actor=b, at most 32 for each filter. A row matches when it has one of the values. An exclude_ filter with several values leaves out the rows with any of them. finding_key also returns each bulk change that included the finding (action bulk_triage). Such a row lists the changed findings in target_ids. order is desc (default) or asc. keep_open is as in /findings. Each row also shows the CVE, image and scanner of the finding or decision that it changed. POST /api/v1/cursors/close session Closes a cursor of /findings or /audit before its last page. Body: {cursor}. It closes the search of the cursor and frees your slot (Exports and reports), and answers 204. A cursor of a different user, of a list that ended, or that expired also gets 204, and nothing changes. A cursor that is not valid gets 422. GET /api/v1/audit/facets session The counts of entity_type, action and actor, with the same filters. The actor counts leave out the actor and exclude_actor filters, so the other users keep their counts. With interval (day or hour) and window_days, it also gives activity: the events in each interval. GET /api/v1/audit/export.csv can_export The audit log as CSV, with the same filters. A file larger than JAVV_EXPORT_MAX_ROWS rows gets 413. GET /api/v1/images session The running images: the images of the last committed inventory. It also shows images with no findings. If JAVV has no committed inventory, inventory is null. GET /api/v1/images/timeline session The scan history of one image tag. image_repo and tag are necessary. GET /api/v1/clusters session The clusters (The clusters list)

items.title: Filters
items.text:
/findings, /findings/facets, /findings/groups, the findings exports and the saved views take the same filters:

Filter What it selects severity critical, high, medium, low, negligible or unknown. The facet uses the same words. A row also shows the word of its scanner in severity. state open, acknowledged, not_affected, risk_accepted, resolved or stale scanner, image_digest The rows with that value namespace, ptype, assignee, image_repo, cve_id, package_name The rows with one of the values. Give the parameter one time for each value, for example namespace=a&namespace=b. Each filter takes at most 32 values. A row in more than one namespace matches each of its namespaces. kev, fixable, disagree true or false present true (default): the findings in the last scan. false: the findings that are gone. new_within_days The findings first seen in the last 1 to 365 days overdue true or false, from the SLA policy at the time of the request. A change of the policy changes the result at once. unassigned true: the rows with no owner. An empty assignee counts as no owner. q 2 to 128 characters. It finds the rows where cve_id, image_repo, namespaces, assignee or package_name contains the text, in any case.
  • Each filter except kev, fixable, disagree, present, new_within_days, overdue, unassigned, image_digest and q has an exclude_ form, for example exclude_severity. An exclude_ filter leaves out the rows with that value. A row with no value for the field stays. Thus exclude_assignee=bob keeps the rows with no owner. An exclude_ filter with more than one value leaves out the rows with any of the values.
  • package_name is not a facet. fields=package_name gets 422.
  • In a saved view (preset) and in a report (params), the filters that take more than one value (namespace, ptype, assignee, image_repo, cve_id, package_name and their exclude_ forms) also take one string. JAVV keeps it as a list with that one value.
  • One field takes the filter or its exclude_ form, not both. assignee and unassigned also do not go together. Each of these pairs gets 422, also in a saved view and in a report.

items.title: A past time: as_of
items.text:
Each read takes as_of. With no value, now or a time in the future, the read shows the current state. With a time in the past, JAVV builds the state at that time from the history:

  • kev, epss, disagree, image_repo, tag and app are not in the history. They are null in the rows.
  • The SLA deadline (overdue and due_at) uses the KEV value that each scan recorded, as a read now does. A scan that JAVV received before release 0.9.1 has no KEV value in the history. A finding from such a scan gets the deadline of its severity.
  • A filter, sort or group on one of these fields gets 422. image_repo and exclude_image_repo get 422 too.
  • A facet on one of these fields gives no values.
  • ptype, package_name and the exclude_ filters on recorded fields apply as usual.
  • The CSV and VEX exports of findings get 501. A report (POST /api/v1/reports) can use a past as_of_t.
  • The audit log and the failed pushes end their window at that time.

items.title: Trends
items.text:
• /trends/scans: the committed scans. interval is day (default) or hour. hour is possible only for 31 days or less, else 422. At a past as_of, the intervals are days.
  • /trends/findings: the new findings and the resolved findings. resolved counts only the findings that a scan no longer showed (resolved_semantics: "scan_resolved"). A triage to resolved does not count. split is scanner (default) or severity. split=severity gets 422 at a past as_of. scanner (trivy or grype) limits the series to one scanner.
  • /trends/ingest-failures: the same days and interval as /trends/scans, so the two series align. It gives {series: {<scanner>: [{date, count}]}, days, interval}. With no refused push, series is {}.

items.title: Failed pushes
items.text: GET /api/v1/scanners/ingest-failures gives {data, total, next_cursor}. Each row has @timestamp, failure_id, scanner, stage, reason, status, error and image_ref. The ingest rejected log line has the same failure_id. The read uses no point in time. Thus a push that fails during your read can show on a later page.

items.title: The clusters list
items.text:
GET /api/v1/clusters gives each cluster that has a token, a name or a retirement record. cluster_name is a name to show. JAVV never uses it in a query. Without a name, it is the cluster_id. Each row has:

  • retired. A retired cluster is in the list only with ?include_retired=true. A cluster that sent a scan after its retirement is not retired.
  • last_scan_at: the newest accepted scan, or null.
  • silent_since: the start of the retirement countdown. This is the newest accepted scan, else the first token, or the return from retirement if that is later.
  • warns_at and retires_at. null means that the cluster never retires.
  • delete_started: true when a delete of the cluster started and did not finish. Delete it again.
  • retirement_mode: manual or auto for a retired cluster, else null. A manual retirement revoked the tokens. To bring the cluster back, make a new token.

items.title: Findings: triage and decisions
items.text: Method Path Access What it does PATCH /api/v1/findings/{finding_key}/triage can_triage Changes the state of one finding: open, acknowledged, not_affected, risk_accepted or resolved. not_affected needs a vex_justification. risk_accepted also needs can_accept_audit_final. A change of state of a risk-accepted finding also needs can_accept_audit_final. This includes a stale finding that goes back to risk_accepted when the scanner reports it again. A change of notes or assignee only does not need it. POST /api/v1/findings/bulk-triage can_triage Changes the state of all the findings that a selector finds, now. More than JAVV_BULK_INLINE_LIMIT (5000) findings get 413. Use a report for more. A selector that finds more than JAVV_BULK_MAX_TARGETS (10000) gets 413. An empty selector gets 422. A change of state of a set that holds risk-accepted findings needs can_accept_audit_final. Without it, the request gets 403 with the count, and JAVV changes no finding. POST /api/v1/decisions can_triage Makes a decision. A risk_accepted or ignore_rule decision also needs can_accept_audit_final. expiry is a date (YYYY-MM-DD), or a date and time with a time zone. JAVV keeps a date and time in UTC. A date stops at 00:00 UTC on that day. Thus the date must be after today in UTC, and a date and time must be after now. Else the answer is 422. GET /api/v1/decisions session Lists the decisions of the cluster, with cve_id, include_revoked (default false), size (1 to 500, default 50) and offset (0 to 10000) PATCH /api/v1/decisions/{decision_id} can_triage Changes a decision. JAVV never changes a decision. It revokes the old one and makes a new one, at the same time. A change from or to risk_accepted or ignore_rule also needs can_accept_audit_final. The new decision keeps the old expiry when the change does not set one. When that expiry is not in the future, the answer is 422, as for POST. POST /api/v1/decisions/{decision_id}/revoke can_triage Revokes a decision. Its effect on the findings stops. A risk_accepted or ignore_rule decision also needs can_accept_audit_final. GET /api/v1/decisions/approvals can_accept_audit_final The approvals queue: the active risk acceptances, the nearest expiry first (The approvals queue) GET /api/v1/decisions/approvals/export.csv can_accept_audit_final and can_export The approvals queue as CSV, with the same filters (The approvals queue)

items.title: The approvals queue
items.text:
GET /api/v1/decisions/approvals takes size and offset, and these filters:

  • q: a part of the CVE id.
  • status: active, expiring, expired or open-ended. JAVV calculates it from expiry at the time of the request. warn_days (default 7) sets when expiring starts.
  • created_by.
  • scanner: both, trivy or grype.

status and created_by take several values, for example status=expired&status=expiring, at most 32 for each filter. An acceptance matches when it has one of the values. q and scanner take one value. Each filter except q has an exclude_ form. An exclude_ filter with several values leaves out the acceptances with any of them. The answer also has facets: the counts of status, created_by and scanner with the same filters. The created_by counts leave out the created_by and exclude_created_by filters, so the other approvers keep their counts. A revoked acceptance is never in the queue.

The CSV export has the same rows. A file larger than JAVV_EXPORT_MAX_ROWS rows gets 413. Two columns are different from the screen:

  • JAVV calculates status for each row, with the same rules as the status filter.
  • scope_namespaces and scope_images give the full lists. If both are empty, the acceptance applies to the full cluster.

items.title: Settings
items.text:
Method Path Access What it does GET /api/v1/settings/sla session The SLA policy: critical_days, high_days, medium_days, low_days and kev_days PUT /api/v1/settings/sla can_manage_settings Replaces the SLA policy GET /api/v1/settings/staleness session The staleness timers for ?cluster_id: the value for the cluster, else the value for all clusters. per_cluster_override shows which one applies. PUT /api/v1/settings/staleness can_manage_settings Replaces the staleness timers. With cluster_id in the body, for that cluster. Without it, for all clusters. GET /api/v1/settings/retirement session The retirement window for ?cluster_id: retire_after_days (null means never) and warn_days, with per_cluster_override PUT /api/v1/settings/retirement can_manage_settings Sets retire_after_days and warn_days. Both are necessary. cluster_id in the body applies as for staleness. A window that is not longer than the scanner-down timer gets 422. A warn_days that is not shorter than the window gets 422. GET /api/v1/settings/scan-scope session The scan scope of ?cluster_id PUT /api/v1/scan-scope can_manage_settings Replaces the scan scope of a cluster: include_namespaces, ignore_namespaces, exclude_images and ignore_kinds. An empty include list means all namespaces. An ignore entry wins over an include entry. GET /api/v1/settings/data can_manage_retention The data settings for ?cluster_id: retention, rollover, export lifetime, findings cleanup and the snapshot repository PUT /api/v1/settings/retention can_manage_retention Sets retention_days. cluster_id in the body applies as for staleness. PUT /api/v1/settings/rollover can_manage_retention Sets max_age_days, max_docs and max_size_gb. cluster_id in the body applies as for staleness. PUT /api/v1/settings/report-ttl can_manage_retention Sets the export lifetime in hours, for all clusters PUT /api/v1/settings/findings-cleanup can_manage_retention Sets cleanup_days: how long a finding that is gone stays. cluster_id in the body applies as for staleness.

Configuring JAVV gives the defaults and the limits of each runtime setting.

items.title: Clusters
items.text: Method Path Access What it does PUT /api/v1/clusters/{cluster_id}/name can_manage_settings Changes the name that JAVV shows for a cluster. The cluster_id never changes. POST /api/v1/clusters/{cluster_id}/retire can_manage_settings Retires a cluster. It leaves the cluster list, and JAVV revokes its tokens. JAVV keeps its data. A cluster that does not exist gets 404. A retired cluster gets 409. POST /api/v1/clusters/{cluster_id}/unretire can_manage_settings Brings a retired cluster back to the list. Its tokens stay revoked. The retirement countdown starts again. A cluster that is not retired gets 409. A cluster with a delete that did not finish gets 409. DELETE /api/v1/clusters/{cluster_id} can_manage_retention Deletes a retired cluster (Delete a cluster)

items.title: Delete a cluster
items.text:
DELETE /api/v1/clusters/{cluster_id} deletes all the data of a retired cluster, except its rows in the audit log. Snapshots from before keep the data.

  1. It writes a marker for the delete.
  2. It deletes the tokens of the cluster. A scanner that still pushes gets 401.
  3. It deletes the history indices of the cluster.
  4. It deletes the rows of the cluster in findings, javv-scan-watermarks, javv-scan-orders, system-decisions, system-notifications and system-reports.
  5. It deletes the settings and the name of the cluster, then its retirement record.

  6. It marks the delete as finished.

  7. A cluster that is not retired gets 409. A cluster that does not exist gets 404.

  8. If an admin brings the cluster back while the delete starts, only one of the two goes ahead. When the delete loses, it gets 409 and deletes nothing. When the bring back loses, it gets 409, and the delete continues.
  9. If a step cannot finish, or OpenSearch is not available, the request gets 503. Send the request again. The delete continues from the step that stopped.
  10. The answer is {cluster_id, deleted: {<what>: count}}.
  11. The marker stays. Each night, the retirement sweep deletes the rows that a push wrote after the delete. Before it deletes them, it writes an audit row with their counts. After a second pass with no rows, or if the cluster comes back, the sweep deletes the marker. A new token for the cluster's ID also deletes the marker: the cluster is back, and JAVV keeps its new data.
  12. A second delete of the same ID, after the cluster came back, writes its own marker.

items.title: Saved views
items.text: Method Path Access What it does GET /api/v1/views session Lists the saved views. Each user can see each view. POST /api/v1/views session Saves a view. You are its owner. preset takes the filters. A value that is not valid gets 422, and so does a pair that Findings refuses. workbench keeps the table setup: columns, dense, sort, order and window_days. PATCH /api/v1/views/{view_id} session, the owner or can_manage_settings Changes the name, the description, preset or workbench. A preset gets the same checks as on POST. A different user gets 403. A change by a different request first gets 409. DELETE /api/v1/views/{view_id} session, the owner or can_manage_settings Deletes a view (204). The audit log keeps a copy of it.

items.title: Dashboards
items.text:
A dashboard is a layout of panels. It holds no data: each panel gets its data with the permissions of the user who opens the dashboard.

Method Path Access What it does GET /api/v1/dashboards session Lists the dashboards that you can see, at most 1,000, by name GET /api/v1/dashboards/{dashboard_id} session One dashboard. A dashboard that you cannot see gets 404, as a dashboard that does not exist. POST /api/v1/dashboards can_edit_dashboards Saves a new dashboard (201). You are its owner. It is private if the body does not set sharing. A name in roles that is not the name of a role gets 422 (unknown_role). PATCH /api/v1/dashboards/{dashboard_id} can_edit_dashboards, the owner or can_manage_settings Changes the fields in the body. The body must have the revision that you read. A different revision gets 409. A user who can see the dashboard, but is not its owner, gets 403. To stop the sharing with roles, send the new sharing and "roles": [] together. A change that sends no panels keeps the stored panels. A name in roles that is not the name of a role gets 422 (unknown_role). A change that sends no roles keeps the stored roles, and does not examine them. DELETE /api/v1/dashboards/{dashboard_id} can_edit_dashboards, the owner or can_manage_settings Deletes the dashboard (204). The query parameter revision is the revision that you read. A different revision gets 409. The audit log keeps a copy of it. GET /api/v1/dashboards/roles can_edit_dashboards The names of the roles that you can share a dashboard with, sorted: {"roles": ["admin", ...]}. It gives no capabilities. /api/v1/admin/roles gives them and needs can_manage_users. GET /api/v1/dashboards/export.ndjson session A file of the dashboards that you can see, at most 1,000. Give one dashboard_id for each dashboard, or no dashboard_id for all of them. See "Dashboard files". POST /api/v1/dashboards/import can_edit_dashboards Makes a dashboard from each line of a file (200, with a result for each line). With copy=true, each line gets a new ID. See "Dashboard files".

Who can see a dashboard:

  • sharing: private: the owner only
  • sharing: everyone: each user
  • sharing: roles: the users with one of the roles in roles
  • a user with can_manage_settings: each dashboard

The fields that you set:

Field Values name 1 to 128 characters description At most 1,024 characters scanner all (default), trivy or grype: the scanner that the dashboard opens with sharing private (default), everyone or roles roles The roles that can see the dashboard, with sharing: roles only. At least one. panels At most 24 panels

Each panel:

Field Values panel The panel ID, for example findings-summary. openapi.json lists the IDs. x The column: 0 (left) or 1 (right) y The row of the top of the panel: 0 to 1,000 w The width: 1 (one column) or 2 (both columns). x + w is at most 2. h The height: short or tall. Each panel has the heights that its catalog entry gives. scanner dashboard (default), trivy or grype, only on a panel with scanner data. dashboard follows the scanner switch of the dashboard.

The backend refuses with 422:

  • a field that is not in these lists, or a panel ID that it does not know
  • a height that the panel does not have, or a scanner on a panel with no scanner data
  • a panel outside the two columns, or two panels on the same cell
  • roles without sharing: roles, or sharing: roles without a role

JAVV writes owner, created_by, created_at, updated_by, updated_at and revision. Each change adds 1 to revision. The audit log has a row for each change (dashboard_create, dashboard_update and dashboard_delete).

items.title: Dashboard files
items.text:
A dashboard file is NDJSON: one dashboard on each line, then one summary line. A line has dashboard_id, schema_version, name, description, scanner, panels, sharing and roles. A line has no owner, user names or times. The summary line is {"exported_count": N, "missing_ids": [...]}. A missing ID is an ID that does not exist or a dashboard that you cannot see. The export does not need can_export.

The export sorts the dashboards by name. Without dashboard_id, it gives the first 1,000, and the summary line does not tell if there are more. The IDs are in the URL: each ID adds approximately 45 characters. A URL longer than 16 KB (approximately 350 IDs) gets 431 from the frontend server.

The import reads the file as the body of the request, with Content-Type: application/x-ndjson. A different type gets 415.

  • You are the owner of each dashboard that the import makes. The audit log gets a dashboard_create row for each one.
  • The import ignores owner, created_by, created_at, updated_by, updated_at and revision in a line. JAVV sets them.
  • Each line gets the checks of POST /api/v1/dashboards. A dashboard_id has 32 lower-case hexadecimal characters. A line must be UTF-8. The import ignores a byte order mark at the start of a line. An object in a line has at most 14 fields. A field that is in an object two times counts two times.
  • A line can have a role from a different JAVV. If this JAVV has no role with that name, the line gets 422 (unknown_role), and the line does not make a dashboard.
  • A line ends at a line feed (\n). The import ignores a \r before it. It skips empty lines and the summary line of an export.
  • The result of a line is 201 (made), 409 (the ID exists) or 422 (the line is not valid). A 422 gives the place and the reason of each error, not the value of the file.
  • With copy=true, each line gets a new ID, so no line gets 409.
  • A file larger than JAVV_DASHBOARD_IMPORT_MAX_BYTES gets 413. A file with more than 1,000 lines that are not empty also gets 413, also when some of those lines are not valid. The summary line of an export is not in this count. After a 413, the import makes no dashboard.
  • A line that makes a dashboard is 3 requests to OpenSearch. 100 such lines take approximately 5 seconds.
  • If OpenSearch refuses a write, the import stops and the answer is the error (for example 429 or 503), without the results. The lines before that line have their dashboards. To complete an import without copy, send the same file again: the dashboards that exist get 409. To complete an import with copy=true, count the dashboards that the import made: you are the owner, and their created_at is after the start of the import. The import writes the lines in the order of the file. Thus, delete that number of valid lines from the start of the file, and send the other lines with copy=true.

The answer has results and the counts created, conflicts and invalid. Each result has line and status. A 201 or 409 result also has dashboard_id, and a 422 result has errors.

items.title: Exports and reports
items.text:
Method Path Access What it does GET /api/v1/findings/export.csv can_export The findings of the filters as CSV. More than JAVV_EXPORT_MAX_ROWS (50000) rows get 413. Make the filter narrower, or use a report. GET /api/v1/findings/export.vex can_export The findings as an OpenVEX or CycloneDX document, for one scanner. scanner is necessary. The row limit is the same. POST /api/v1/reports can_export for export, can_triage for bulk_triage Puts a job in the queue and answers 201. Its params take the filters of GET /api/v1/findings and refuse the same pairs with 422: a filter with its exclude_ side, and assignee with unassigned. kind: bulk_triage needs can_triage, and can_accept_audit_final for a risk acceptance or for a change of state of a set that holds risk-accepted findings. A bulk triage keeps the list of findings at this time. If the user does not have can_accept_audit_final, the job checks the set again before it changes a finding. When a finding became risk-accepted after the request, the job fails and changes no finding. Only the JAVV_BULK_MAX_TARGETS limit applies. Its patch takes the fields of POST /api/v1/findings/bulk-triage (state, vex_justification, assignee and notes), with the same limits. A different field gets 422. JAVV does not change a field whose value is null. GET /api/v1/reports/{report_id} session, the owner The status of your job. A job of a different user gets 404. When the job is done and not expired, the answer has a download_token for 15 minutes. GET /api/v1/reports/{report_id}/download can_export, the owner, and token Downloads the result. After expires_at, the request gets 410. With no result yet, it gets 404. A wrong or expired token gets 403.

In each CSV file, JAVV puts an apostrophe before a cell that starts with =, +, -, @, a tab or a carriage return. Thus a spreadsheet does not run the cell as a formula.

Each user can have JAVV_MAX_CONCURRENT_PITS_PER_PRINCIPAL (default 10) open cursors and exports at the same time. One more gets 429 with Retry-After. A cursor is open from its first page until its last page, until you close it with POST /api/v1/cursors/close, or until JAVV_SEARCH_PIT_KEEP_ALIVE plus 30 seconds after the last page that you read. JAVV keeps the result of a report in OpenSearch for JAVV_EXPORT_TTL_HOURS (default 24). The report_drain job runs the queue, on JAVV_JOB_REPORT_DRAIN_CRON (default every 5 minutes). A result larger than JAVV_EXPORT_MAX_BYTES makes the job fail. Before a bulk triage job writes, it checks its patch again. A patch that is not valid makes the job fail, and the error of the job names the field, not its value. At the end of a job, a report_ready notification goes to the user.

items.title: Notifications
items.text:
Method Path Access What it does GET /api/v1/notifications session Your 50 newest notifications, and unread, the count of the unread ones. Each item has cluster_name: the name of its cluster now, the cluster_id if the cluster has no name, or null if the item has no cluster. PATCH /api/v1/notifications/{notification_id}/read session Marks one of your notifications as read. A notification of a different user gets 404. DELETE /api/v1/notifications/{notification_id} session Deletes one of your notifications (204). A notification of a different user gets 404.

The types are report_ready, sla_breach, assignment and cluster_retiring:

  • The retirement sweep sends cluster_retiring to each user with can_manage_settings when a cluster starts its warning period. It sends it one time for each silence. ref is the retires_at of the cluster.
  • The sweep deletes these notifications when the cluster scans again, or when a return from retirement starts a new silence. A change of the settings keeps them.

items.title: Ingest a scan
items.text:
POST /api/v1/ingest/scan accepts the results of one scan: an envelope with schema_version 3 or 4, as JSON. The body can have Content-Encoding: gzip. The findings of a version 3 envelope have ptype: null. Push from your own script gives the schema, the order of the calls and an example.
