items.title: Upgrading JAVV
items.text:
This page tells you how to move a running JAVV to a newer release:

  • What to check before you start.
  • The sequence of the upgrade, with docker compose or with Helm.
  • How to check the result, and how to go back to the previous release.

JAVV has three parts. You upgrade each part separately:

Part What changes its version Where to find the version Backend (FastAPI) The JAVV release The release tag. GET /api/v1/meta → version Frontend (Vue) The JAVV release, together with the backend The same release Scanner images (Trivy, Grype) You change the published image tag in your deployment versions.yaml lists the supported scanner versions

JAVV never changes a version in a cluster that you scan. You set each version as a tag in your own deployment. To install JAVV, see DEPLOYING.md.

items.title: Before you upgrade
items.text:
1. Read the release notes. Each release has a GitHub Release and an entry in CHANGELOG.md. Then read Version notes on this page. They tell you what a release needs from you.
  2. Make a snapshot. The upgrade does not need it.
    • Use Settings › Data & OpenSearch › Snapshot now, or POST /api/v1/admin/snapshots. The request needs can_manage_retention.
    • The request returns 409 when OpenSearch has no snapshot repository. Snapshots tells you how to add the repository.
    • The snapshot keeps the current state, the triage, the decisions, the users, the settings and the audit log. It does not keep the scan history that time travel reads. Thus a restore does not bring the history back.
  3. Check the OpenSearch version. CI tests JAVV with the version in datastore.opensearch in versions.yaml.

items.title: Sequence of the upgrade
items.text:
Upgrade the backend first, then the frontend, then the scanner images.

  1. Backend. Each new backend pod upgrades the indices when it starts.
    • It compares each index and template with the schema version of the release, and it adds the missing parts.
    • It opens its port only after this step. Thus it receives no requests before its indices are ready.
    • You do not need to do a step manually.
  2. Frontend. Upgrade it together with the backend, or immediately after the backend. A newer frontend can send requests that an older backend does not have.
  3. Scanner images. Change the Trivy and Grype image tags after the backend runs the new release. A newer scanner can send a report format (schema_version) that only the newer backend accepts. GET /api/v1/meta → envelope_versions lists the formats that the backend accepts.

There is only one backend, and an upgrade replaces it. Thus two backend releases never run at the same time.

After you go back to an older release, an older backend reads indices that a newer backend changed. This is safe, because each schema change until now only added fields:

  • An older backend ignores the fields that it does not know.
  • A newer backend reads a missing field as empty.

items.title: With docker compose
items.text:
Prerequisites:

  • Your .env file. Keep it: it holds your settings.
  • The compose.yaml of the new release. It names the backend and frontend images of that release.
  • A copy of your changes to compose.yaml, for example the host port. Make the same changes in the new file.

Steps:

  1. In the folder of your installation, keep a copy of the old file, and get the file of the new release. VERSION is the release that you upgrade to: 
    VERSION=0.9.0
cp compose.yaml compose.yaml.old
curl -fsSLO "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Danube-Labs/javv-poc/v$VERSION/deploy/compose/compose.yaml"
  2. Make your changes to compose.yaml again, if you had changes.
  3. Pull the images and start them: 
    docker compose pull
docker compose up -d

JAVV is not available for some seconds, while the new backend starts and upgrades the indices. The frontend waits until the backend reports healthy (depends_on).

To go back to the previous release, put the compose.yaml of that release back (compose.yaml.old), and run the two commands of step 3. To go back to a release before 0.7.0, first put back the old name of the secret key (Go back to a previous release).

items.title: Upgrade from 0.5.1 to 0.6.1 or later
items.text:
From 0.6.0, OpenSearch requires a sign-in. 0.6.0 published no images, so use 0.6.1 or later. Before step 3, add these two values to your .env:

  • JAVV_OPENSEARCH_ADMIN_PASSWORD: the password of the OpenSearch admin.
  • JAVV_OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD: the password of javv, the user that the backend signs in as.

The compose file does not start without these two values. OpenSearch refuses a weak admin password. DEPLOYING.md gives the rules.

Your data stays:

  • When OpenSearch first starts with its sign-in on, it keeps each index, and it adds its security configuration.
  • You can also go back to a 0.5.x compose.yaml with the same data. Then OpenSearch runs without its sign-in again.

We did these steps on the real compose files, from a 0.5.1 installation with data.

items.title: Change an OpenSearch password
items.text:
OpenSearch reads JAVV_OPENSEARCH_ADMIN_PASSWORD and JAVV_OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD only on its first start with its sign-in on. It keeps the two passwords in its data. Thus OpenSearch ignores a new value in .env:

  • With a new admin password, OpenSearch never reports healthy, because its healthcheck uses the new value. The backend waits for OpenSearch, and docker compose up -d fails after some minutes.
  • With a new javv password, the backend stops with "refused the credentials in JAVV_OPENSEARCH_USERNAME".

To change a password and keep the data:

  1. Put the new password in .env.
  2. Start only OpenSearch: docker compose up -d opensearch. It still accepts only the old password.
  3. Load the new password into the security index of OpenSearch. Use the demo admin certificate in the image: 
    docker compose exec opensearch plugins/opensearch-security/tools/securityadmin.sh \
  -f config/opensearch-security/internal_users.yml -t internalusers -icl -nhnv \
  -cacert config/root-ca.pem -cert config/kirk.pem -key config/kirk-key.pem
    The command ends with Done with success. The compose file writes internal_users.yml from .env at each start. Thus the file holds the two new passwords.
  4. Run docker compose up -d.

Other methods do not work, or delete data:

  • docker compose down -v also makes OpenSearch use a new password. But it deletes all JAVV data.
  • The account API of OpenSearch cannot change the admin password: admin is a reserved user (403).

items.title: Only for OpenSearch started from a main checkout: load the missing users
items.text:
Do these steps only when the security index of OpenSearch holds only admin. No release made this state. A main checkout before 0.6.0 can make it, because OpenSearch reads the files for users, roles and role mappings only on its first start with its sign-in on.

  1. In .env, move the value of JAVV_OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD to JAVV_OPENSEARCH_ADMIN_PASSWORD. In this state, JAVV_OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD was the admin password.
  2. Give JAVV_OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD a new value. This is the password of javv.
  3. Start only OpenSearch: docker compose up -d opensearch.
  4. Load the three files one time, with the same certificate: 
    for f in internal_users:internalusers roles:roles roles_mapping:rolesmapping; do
  docker compose exec opensearch plugins/opensearch-security/tools/securityadmin.sh \
    -f "config/opensearch-security/${f%%:*}.yml" -t "${f#*:}" -icl -nhnv \
    -cacert config/root-ca.pem -cert config/kirk.pem -key config/kirk-key.pem
done
    Each file ends with Done with success. Sometimes the tool then shows a java.nio.channels.ClosedSelectorException. This message comes from the HTTP client of the tool when it closes, after the load. You can ignore it.
  5. Run docker compose up -d.

The same loop loads a changed javv role. If a release changes the role, its notes tell you. We did these steps on the real compose files, from an OpenSearch that a main checkout started.

items.title: On Kubernetes (Helm)
items.text:
Each release publishes the JAVV chart and the OpenSearch chart (DEPLOYING.md) at oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts, with the version of the release.

Prerequisites:

  • Your settings in your own values files. An install with --set, as in DEPLOYING.md, writes no values file. Thus, before the first upgrade, write the values of each release to a file: 
    helm get values store -o yaml > my-store-values.yaml
helm get values javv -o yaml > my-javv-values.yaml
helm get values scanner -n javv-scanner -o yaml > my-scanner-values.yaml   # in each scanned cluster
  • These files hold each value that you set, the passwords included. Keep them as safe as your Secrets.

Steps:

  1. Upgrade with the chart of the new release and the same files. VERSION is the release that you upgrade to: 
    VERSION=0.9.0
helm upgrade store oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts/javv-opensearch --version "$VERSION" \
  -f my-store-values.yaml
helm upgrade javv oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts/javv --version "$VERSION" -f my-javv-values.yaml
helm test javv
    • Do the store upgrade when the release changed the OpenSearch chart. Version notes tells you which releases did.
    • It is safe to do it when the chart did not change. Then the upgrade changes only labels, and OpenSearch does not restart.
  2. Upgrade the scanners last, in each cluster that you scan, after JAVV runs the new release. Keep your values file (backendUrl and the token Secrets): 
    VERSION=0.9.0
helm upgrade scanner oci://ghcr.io/danube-labs/charts/javv-scanner --version "$VERSION" \
  -n javv-scanner -f my-scanner-values.yaml
    • A newer scanner can send a report format that only the newer backend accepts.
    • The javv-scanner chart holds the scanner versions of its release.
    • When the refresh container changes, the upgrade starts a vuln-DB refresh. The refresh container changes with the image, the DB source, extraEnv, resources or pullPolicy.
    • The next cycle uses the new image.

While the backend restarts:

  • The backend runs as one pod with strategy: Recreate. The backend runs the background jobs, so two backends must never run at the same time. Kubernetes stops the old pod before it starts the new pod.
  • JAVV is not available for some seconds, while the new pod checks OpenSearch and upgrades the indices. The startup probe gives this step 300 seconds.
  • During this time, the frontend replies 502, and the web app shows "backend not answering".
  • Kubernetes replaces the frontend with no gap.

To go back to a previous revision, use one command. helm history javv lists the revisions:

helm rollback javv          # to the revision before the current one
helm rollback javv 3        # or to a specific revision
  • The settings and the images of that revision come back.
  • The indices stay as the newer release left them, and an older backend can read them (Go back to a previous release).
  • CI does an upgrade and a rollback for each change to the charts.
  • For the scanners, run helm rollback scanner in each scanned cluster. Do this before you go back to the previous JAVV release.

To change an OpenSearch password (of admin, or of javv, the user that the backend signs in as), see the javv-opensearch chart README.

  • After you change the javv password, restart the backend. Then it reads the new password from the same Secret: kubectl rollout restart deploy/javv-backend.
  • The same section of the README tells you how to load the javv role and its mapping into an OpenSearch that first started without them.

items.title: Check what runs
items.text:
Check Where Expected result OpenSearch replies GET /readyz (no sign-in) 200 The versions that run GET /api/v1/meta (with a signed-in session) {"version": "<release>", "mapping_version": <n>, "envelope_versions": [...]} The versions that run, in the web app The bottom of the sidebar Three lines: v<release>, store schema v<n>, scanner schema v<n> What the upgrade did The backend log, one line for each pod start The event bootstrap complete, with app_version, mapping_version, and the indices in created, updated or unchanged The scanners use the new version The Scanner status page, after the next scan cycle The new scanner version for each cluster

On the first start of a new release, updated lists the indices whose schema changed. Later starts list all indices as unchanged.

items.title: Go back to a previous release
items.text:
• The indices stay safe when you go back to an older backend. The index setup changes indices only to a newer schema. An older release finds the indices at a newer schema version, and it does not change them. The fields that the newer release added stay, and the older release does not use them.
  • The older release can read the settings that the newer release saved. The newer release can add a field to a setting. If you saved that setting, the older release ignores the new field. The backend logs stored setting has unknown keys one time for each setting. It counts each of these reads in javv_stored_setting_unknown_fields_total (API.md § Metrics). If you save that setting while the older release runs, the older release saves only the fields that it knows. After you upgrade again, the new field has its default value. This is true when you go back to 0.4.8 or later.
  • Go back with the scanners first when the report format changed between the two releases. Then the scanners do not send a format that the older backend refuses.
  • A release before 0.7.0 needs the old name of the secret key. These releases read JAVV_TOKEN_PEPPER (docker compose) or the key token-pepper of secrets.existingSecret (Helm). If you deleted it after the upgrade to 0.7.0, put it back with the same value before you go back:
    • docker compose: sed -n 's/^JAVV_SECRET_KEY=/JAVV_TOKEN_PEPPER=/p' .env >> .env. Without it, docker compose up stops with set JAVV_TOKEN_PEPPER in .env, and the newer release continues to run.
    • Helm with secrets.existingSecret: copy the value of secret-key into token-pepper. Without it, helm rollback javv succeeds, but the older backend pod does not start (couldn't find key token-pepper in Secret). JAVV is not available until you copy the value. 
      kubectl patch secret <your-secret> --type merge -p \
  "{\"data\":{\"token-pepper\":\"$(kubectl get secret <your-secret> -o jsonpath='{.data.secret-key}')\"}}"
  • CI tests a rollback from each change to the last release. On a new docker compose store, CI starts the last release and writes data with it. Then CI starts the change, the last release again, and the change again. After each start, CI signs in and reads the same findings and the same SLA policy.
  • A snapshot does not give a rollback in one step. A restore makes restored-* copies next to the live indices. It never writes over them (POST /api/v1/admin/snapshots/{snapshot_name}/restore). To use a copy, you must move it into place manually.

items.title: The first run of the background jobs
items.text:
From 0.5.0, the backend starts its own background jobs. On an installation that ran these jobs only manually, or never, the first scheduled runs do all the work at the same time:

  • The lifecycle sweep (03:00 by default) deletes all scan history that is older than the retention of each cluster (90 days by default). After this, time travel cannot show that period. Before the jobs run for the first time, see what the sweep will do: Data inspector › Repair actions › Lifecycle sweep › Dry run. If it deletes more than you want, increase the retention in Settings › Data & OpenSearch.
  • The staleness sweep (02:00) marks as stale each finding that no scan found again for 3 days. It also marks as stale all findings of a scanner that sent nothing for 7 days.
  • The findings cleanup (04:00) deletes the findings that no scan reported for longer than its period (180 days).

A job does not run because the backend started. Each job waits for its next scheduled time.

  • To stop all the jobs, start the backend with JAVV_SCHEDULER_ENABLED=false.
  • To stop one job, set its JAVV_JOB_<KIND>_CRON to an empty value.
  • Job schedules and the time zone gives the schedules, and the time zone that the backend uses for them.

If you ran these jobs from your own cron or from CronJobs, delete them. The scheduler of the backend replaces them. If both run, nothing breaks: the backend does not start a job that is already running. But the second run is work for no result.

items.title: Version notes
items.text:
A release gets an entry here when it needs something from you. These are the conditions:

  • The store schema changed (mapping_version).
  • The report formats that the backend accepts changed (envelope_versions).
  • The scanner images must be published again, or changed together with the release.
  • The OpenSearch chart (javv-opensearch) changed. Then do the store upgrade.

The entries start with 0.6. Before 0.6, each schema change only added fields, and the backend applied it automatically on the first start.

Release Store schema Report formats accepted What to do 0.9.1 20 3 and 4 Nothing. The backend adds a field to the store on the first start. 0.8.9 19 3 and 4 The notes A new permission for the export files and A new permission for dashboards below 0.8.7 18 3 and 4 The note JAVV refuses a username with a capital letter below 0.8.0 18 3 and 4 The note A bootstrap admin password longer than 256 characters stops the backend below 0.7.0 18 3 and 4 The note JAVV_TOKEN_PEPPER is now JAVV_SECRET_KEY below 0.6.2 18 3 and 4 The note JAVV retires clusters that send no scans below 0.6.0 18 3 and 4 The note How the backend connects to OpenSearch below

No release from 0.4.8 to 0.8.0 changed the store schema (18) or the report formats that the backend accepts (3 and 4).

No release up to and including 0.9.0 changed the OpenSearch chart in a way that needs the store upgrade. Each release changed its version number. Some releases also changed other parts of the chart, but not OpenSearch:

  • 0.7.1 and 0.8.6 changed the text of its README and of the comments in values.yaml, and no value. 0.8.1 changed the text of its README.
  • 0.8.7 changed the test pod of the chart (helm test store). The pod can now run in a namespace with the restricted level of the pod security standards.

items.title: 0.8.9: a new permission for the export files
items.text:
A user now needs the permission can_export to download a file of the data:

  • the CSV and VEX files of the findings
  • the CSV files of the audit log, the contributors and the approvals queue
  • an export report

Without the permission, these requests get 403. The viewer role does not get it. A viewer can still read the data on the screens and through the API.

A new store gives the permission to the triager, security_lead and admin roles. But JAVV writes the roles only on the first start of a store. Thus on a store that you have, only admin gets the permission, because * holds each permission. Also, each user keeps a copy of the permissions of its role.

After the upgrade, give the permission to the triager and security_lead roles and to their users:

  1. Save this script as can-export.sh, in the folder of your installation: 
    # Adds can_export to the triager and security_lead roles, and to their users.
login=$(printf %s "$OPENSEARCH_INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD" | sed 's/[\\"]/\\&/g')
curl -sSk -K - -X POST 'https://localhost:9200/system-roles,system-users/_update_by_query?refresh=true' \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "query": {"terms": {"role": ["triager", "security_lead"]}},
  "script": {"lang": "painless", "source": "def c = ctx._source.capabilities; if (c == null || c.contains(\"can_export\")) { ctx.op = \"noop\" } else { c.add(\"can_export\") }"}
}' <<EOF
user = "admin:$login"
EOF
echo
  2. Run the script in the OpenSearch container: 
    docker compose exec -T opensearch sh < can-export.sh
    The answer has "failures":[]. updated is the number of roles and users that the script changed. If you run the script again, it changes nothing.

The script reads the admin password in the container, as the health check of the compose file does. Thus the password is not in your shell history or in the arguments of a process. The users do not sign in again: JAVV reads the permissions of a user on each request.

On Kubernetes, or with an OpenSearch of your own, send the same request to your OpenSearch, with its admin.

We did these steps on the compose files of 0.8.8, with a triager and a security lead.

items.title: 0.8.9: a new permission for dashboards
items.text:
A user needs the permission can_edit_dashboards to make a dashboard. The viewer role does not get it.

The store schema is now 19. At its first start, the backend makes the new index system-dashboards. You do not do a step for it. The javv role of an OpenSearch of your own already has access to it, because its name starts with system-.

A new store gives the permission to the triager, security_lead and admin roles. On a store that you have, only admin gets it, because JAVV writes the roles only on the first start of a store. Also, each user keeps a copy of the permissions of its role.

After the upgrade, give the permission to the triager and security_lead roles and to their users:

  1. Save this script as can-edit-dashboards.sh, in the folder of your installation: 
    # Adds can_edit_dashboards to the triager and security_lead roles, and to their users.
login=$(printf %s "$OPENSEARCH_INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD" | sed 's/[\\"]/\\&/g')
curl -sSk -K - -X POST 'https://localhost:9200/system-roles,system-users/_update_by_query?refresh=true' \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "query": {"terms": {"role": ["triager", "security_lead"]}},
  "script": {"lang": "painless", "source": "def c = ctx._source.capabilities; if (c == null || c.contains(\"can_edit_dashboards\")) { ctx.op = \"noop\" } else { c.add(\"can_edit_dashboards\") }"}
}' <<EOF
user = "admin:$login"
EOF
echo
  2. Run the script in the OpenSearch container: 
    docker compose exec -T opensearch sh < can-edit-dashboards.sh
    The answer has "failures":[]. updated is the number of roles and users that the script changed. If you run the script again, it changes nothing.

The users do not sign in again: JAVV reads the permissions of a user on each request.

On Kubernetes, or with an OpenSearch of your own, send the same request to your OpenSearch, with its admin.

We sent the request of the script two times to OpenSearch 3.9.0, with the roles and users of 0.8.8. The first time changed the two roles and their users. The second time changed nothing.

items.title: 0.8.7: JAVV refuses a username with a capital letter
items.text:
A new username must be in lower case. Before 0.8.7, Alice and alice could be two different users. Users that exist keep their names.

  • New users. POST /api/v1/admin/users gives 422 for a username with a capital letter, with the message a username must be in lower case.
  • The first admin. A JAVV_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME with a capital letter stops the backend at each start, also when the first admin exists. The backend shows invalid settings: JAVV_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME: Value error, a username must be in lower case. Then set the name in lower case. If no user has that name, and you set JAVV_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD, the backend makes a new first admin. The old admin stays.
  • Sign-in. A user can type a lower-case username in any case: ALICE signs in as alice. A user whose name has a capital letter, for example Alice, must type the name exactly. The sign-in lock counts the failures of all cases of a name together.

items.title: 0.8.0: a bootstrap admin password longer than 256 characters stops the backend
items.text:
A sign-in accepts a password of 256 characters at most. A first admin with a longer JAVV_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD could never sign in. The backend now refuses such a value at start, and shows invalid settings: JAVV_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD: String should have at most 256 characters. It does this also when the first admin exists, because the backend reads the setting at each start.

If you see this error, set a password of 256 characters or fewer. A new value does not change the password of an admin that exists.

items.title: 0.7.0: JAVV_TOKEN_PEPPER is now JAVV_SECRET_KEY
items.text:
Only the name changes. Keep the same value. A backend that finds the old name stops at start, and it shows the new name. If you change the value:

  • Each scanner gets 401 and needs a new token.
  • Each user must sign in again.

  • Each open download link stops working.

  • docker compose: in .env, add the new name with the same value. Keep the line with the old name until you do not need to go back to a release before 0.7.0: 

    sed -n 's/^JAVV_TOKEN_PEPPER=/JAVV_SECRET_KEY=/p' .env >> .env
    Until you add the new name, docker compose up stops with set JAVV_SECRET_KEY in .env. The compose.yaml of 0.7.0 and later gives only JAVV_SECRET_KEY to the backend. Thus the old name in .env has no effect on it.

  • Helm, with the value in your values file: change the name secrets.tokenPepper to secrets.secretKey, and keep its value. Until you do this, the upgrade stops with additional properties 'tokenPepper' not allowed. If you set the value with --set, write your values to a file first (see On Kubernetes (Helm)). Change the name in my-javv-values.yaml. Then upgrade with -f my-javv-values.yaml.
  • Helm, with secrets.existingSecret: the chart now reads the key secret-key from that Secret. Before the upgrade, copy the value of token-pepper into it: 
    kubectl patch secret <your-secret> --type merge -p \
  "{\"data\":{\"secret-key\":\"$(kubectl get secret <your-secret> -o jsonpath='{.data.token-pepper}')\"}}"
    Keep the key token-pepper until you do not need to go back to a release before 0.7.0. Those releases read only token-pepper. After that, you can delete it.

items.title: 0.6.2: JAVV retires clusters that send no scans
items.text:
A new daily job retires a cluster that sent no accepted scan for 45 days (JAVV_CLUSTER_RETIRE_AFTER_DAYS). A retired cluster is not in the cluster list, in the cluster selector or in All clusters. JAVV keeps all of its data and its tokens. The cluster comes back with its next accepted scan. You can also bring it back manually: POST /api/v1/clusters/{cluster_id}/unretire.

The first run (04:15 by default) retires each cluster that sent no scan for that time. An example is a cluster that you made again: it comes back with a new ID. To keep a cluster, do one of these steps:

  • Set its period to never: PUT /api/v1/settings/retirement with its cluster_id, retire_after_days: null, and warn_days as before.
  • Set JAVV_CLUSTER_RETIRE_AFTER_DAYS=0 to stop retirement for all clusters.

When no cluster had an accepted scan within its scanner-down period, the job retires nothing, and it logs a warning. This condition shows a problem in JAVV, not in the clusters.

items.title: 0.6.0: how the backend connects to OpenSearch
items.text:
There are two changes, both on purpose:

  • A JAVV_OPENSEARCH_URL that holds a user or a password stops the backend at start. Earlier releases sent https://user:pass@host (or user:pass@host, with no scheme) to the client. Move the credentials into JAVV_OPENSEARCH_USERNAME and JAVV_OPENSEARCH_PASSWORD (Connection to OpenSearch).
  • A wrong setting stops the start, with one line for each variable: invalid settings: JAVV_<NAME>: <reason>. The line holds no value from your environment. Earlier releases showed part of the environment, and secrets could be in it.

The token command (python -m backend.core.tokens) and the scan-scope command now also use JAVV_REQUEST_TIMEOUT, as the rest of the backend did before (30 seconds by default).

items.title: Supported versions
items.text:
This page lists the scanner versions and the OpenSearch version that this release of JAVV pins and supports.

JAVV publishes a scanner image for each supported version, as ghcr.io/danube-labs/javv-scanner-{trivy,grype}:<version>. The javv-scanner chart runs the current version. To run a different supported version, set it in the chart.

Component Current Also supported Trivy 0.76.1 0.70.0 Grype 0.120.1 0.114.0 OpenSearch 3.9.0 n/a

items.title: Indices and data
items.text:
This page tells you which OpenSearch indices JAVV uses, what each index holds, and how long JAVV keeps the data. It also tells you what a snapshot holds. For the disk space and the shards that the data needs, see Sizing OpenSearch.

JAVV keeps all of its data in one OpenSearch:

  • The name of each index of JAVV is findings, or it starts with javv- or system-.
  • The javv role of OpenSearch permits only these indices, and the restored-* copies that a restore writes (An OpenSearch of your own).

items.title: See the indices
items.text:
1. Sign in as a user with the permission can_inspect_store.
  2. Open the Data inspector.
  3. Send GET _cat/indices. The answer shows only the indices of JAVV, with the number of documents and the size of each index.

items.title: Change how long JAVV keeps the history
items.text:
1. Sign in as a user with the permission can_manage_retention.
  2. Go to Settings › Data & OpenSearch.

  3. In Retention, set the days for all clusters, or for one cluster.

  4. The lifecycle sweep deletes the history indices that are older than the new retention at its next run (03:00 by default).

  5. After that, time travel cannot show that period.
  6. Retention and rollover gives the settings.

items.title: Back up the data
items.text:
A snapshot from Settings › Data & OpenSearch › Snapshot now:

  • Holds findings, javv-images-* and system-*, except system-sessions. These indices hold the current state, the triage, the decisions, the users, the settings and the audit log.
  • Does not hold the sessions. A sign-out only marks its session as ended, so a restored copy could make an ended session valid again. After a restore, the users sign in again.
  • Does not hold the scan history (javv-finding-occurrences-*, javv-scan-events-*, javv-inventory-runs-* and javv-ingest-failures-*), javv-scan-orders or javv-scan-watermarks. Thus a restore does not bring back the history that time travel reads.

Also:

  • JAVV does not make scheduled snapshots yet.
  • A restore writes restored-* copies, and never writes over the live indices.
  • Snapshots tells you how to set up the snapshot repository.

items.title: The history indices
items.text:
Each cluster has its own series of each of these indices:

  • JAVV makes the first index of a series when the cluster sends its first data.
  • The lifecycle sweep starts a new index in a series at 30 days, 5,000,000 documents or 50 GB, the first limit that the series gets to.
  • The sweep deletes an index when its newest data is older than the retention of the cluster (90 days by default).
  • Each limit is a setting (Retention and rollover).
Index What it holds javv-finding-occurrences-<cluster_id>-* One document for each finding in each scan. Time travel reads it. It holds almost all of the data of JAVV. javv-scan-events-<cluster_id>-* One document for each image and scanner in each scan. It holds the count of each severity, the versions of the scanner and of its database, and the scan settings. javv-images-<cluster_id>-* The images of each scan cycle, with their counts. The Images page reads it. javv-inventory-runs-<cluster_id>-* One document for each scan cycle: the number of images that the scanner expected, and the number that JAVV received. javv-ingest-failures-<cluster_id>-* One document for each push that JAVV refused after the token check. The Failed ingests table reads it.

items.title: The audit log
items.text: Index What it holds How long JAVV keeps it system-audit-log-* One document for each change and each sign-in, with the user and the time JAVV starts a new index at the limits for all clusters (not the limits of one cluster). It never deletes an index of the audit log.

items.title: The current state and the settings
items.text:
Each of these is one index. JAVV makes it at the first start of the backend.

Index What it holds How long JAVV keeps it findings The current state of each finding, with its triage The findings cleanup deletes a finding that no scan found for longer than its window (180 days by default, Findings cleanup). javv-scan-watermarks For each image and scanner, the newest scan that JAVV applied The findings cleanup deletes the document of an image when findings has no row for the image. The last scan of the image must also be older than the cleanup window. javv-scan-orders The scan_order counter of each cluster and scanner JAVV never deletes it. system-decisions The decisions, for example the risk acceptances, also the revoked ones JAVV never deletes them. system-users and system-roles The users and the roles JAVV never deletes them. An admin can disable a user. system-tokens The ingest tokens, as a hash A revoked token stays, disabled. system-sessions The sign-in sessions The session sweep deletes a session 24 hours after it ends (JAVV_SESSION_SWEEP_GRACE_HOURS). system-config The runtime settings, the cluster names and the retirement records Until you change them system-views The saved views Until the owner or a user with can_manage_settings deletes them system-dashboards The saved dashboards: their panels and who can see them Until the owner or a user with can_manage_settings deletes them. Both also need can_edit_dashboards. system-notifications The notifications of the bell Until the user deletes them. The retirement sweep deletes a retirement notice when the cluster scans again. system-reports and system-report-chunks The queued exports and bulk actions, and the results of the exports The report sweep deletes a finished export after the export lifetime (24 hours by default), and a failed job after the same time. system-jobs The last run of each background job One document for each job, which JAVV writes again at each run

items.title: When you delete a cluster
items.text:
A delete of a retired cluster deletes its history indices and its tokens. It also deletes its documents in findings, javv-scan-watermarks, javv-scan-orders, system-decisions, system-notifications, system-reports and system-config. It keeps its rows in the audit log (Delete a cluster).

JAVV never reads the restored-* copies, and it never deletes them. Delete them yourself when you do not need them.

items.title: Scaling and failures
items.text:
This page tells you how many copies of each part of JAVV run, and why. It also tells you how each part recovers when it fails.

JAVV runs as one backend, one frontend and one OpenSearch node:

  • The compose file and the charts install this setup.
  • CI tests this setup.
  • JAVV supports only this setup.

items.title: What the charts run
items.text: Part Copies Can you change the number? Backend (javv chart) 1, with strategy: Recreate No. The chart refuses a backend.replicas value. Nobody tested more than one backend, and JAVV does not support it. Frontend (javv chart) frontend.replicas, 1 by default The chart accepts more than one, because the frontend keeps no state. Nobody tested more than one. OpenSearch (javv-opensearch chart, compose) 1 node No. The chart refuses all other values. For more nodes, use an OpenSearch that you operate. Scanners (javv-scanner chart, in each cluster that you scan) One CronJob for each scanner. Only one cycle runs at a time (concurrencyPolicy: Forbid). No

items.title: Why one backend
items.text:
The backend runs the background jobs of JAVV on schedules:

  • The jobs are staleness, lifecycle, findings cleanup, cluster retirement, report drain, report sweep and session sweep.
  • The schedules are the JAVV_JOB_*_CRON settings in Configuration.
  • No CronJob and no second container runs these jobs. Thus the backend is one process.

A rolling update can run two backends for a short time. To prevent this, the Deployment uses Recreate: Kubernetes stops the old pod before it starts the new pod. During an upgrade, there is a short time when no backend runs:

  • The browsers show a banner that tells you that the backend is not available. The banner goes away when the backend replies again.
  • The scanners try each push again, with a longer wait each time. When all tries fail, a scanner keeps the push in its dead-letter file. In its next cycle, it scans the image again.

items.title: Failures and recovery
items.text:
JAVV has no high-availability layer of its own. Each part is one copy. Kubernetes or docker compose starts the part again when it fails.

  • The backend stops at start when it cannot connect to OpenSearch.
    • Its restart policy starts it again until OpenSearch replies.
    • When OpenSearch stops, the backend reports that it is not ready (/readyz). Then its Service stops sending requests to it, and nothing restarts it.
  • The frontend keeps no state. A new frontend is ready immediately. When a frontend stops during a scanner push, the scanner sends that push again.
  • OpenSearch keeps its data on its volume. When OpenSearch starts again, it reads the data again.
    • To keep the data available when a node fails, you need more nodes and replica shards.
    • For this, use an OpenSearch that you operate. JAVV connects to it with no change. See Deploying: an OpenSearch of your own and Sizing OpenSearch.
  • Backups: make a snapshot manually in Settings › Data & OpenSearch › Snapshots. JAVV does not make scheduled snapshots yet.

items.title: Sizing OpenSearch
items.text:
This page tells you how much shard space, memory and disk OpenSearch needs for your clusters. It also tells you which limit you get to first, and what to change when you get near a limit.

JAVV keeps all of its data in one OpenSearch: the scan results, their history, and each triage decision. The figures marked measured come from one development install: 4 clusters, about 1.7 million documents, OpenSearch 3.9.0 and a 1 GB heap.

items.title: Calculate the size of the history
items.text:
Each scan writes a full copy of what it found. JAVV writes one document for each finding, for each image, for each scanner and for each scan cycle. Time travel reads this history. The history is almost all of the data in OpenSearch.

Index Contents Measured javv-finding-occurrences-<cluster>-* The history: one document for each finding in each scan 1.54 M documents, 436 MB, about 280 bytes each findings The current state of each finding, with its triage 123 k documents, 60 MB, about 490 bytes each javv-scan-events-*, javv-images-*, javv-inventory-runs-*, javv-ingest-failures-* One document for each scan, or for each image in each cycle Less than 6 MB in total system-* Users, sessions, decisions, the audit log, settings and reports Less than 4 MB in total

The sizes are for the primary copy. To calculate the size of the history for your clusters, use these two formulas:

documents per day ≈ for each scanner: images × findings per image × scan cycles per day
history size      ≈ documents per day × (retention days + 30) × 280 bytes

The formula adds 30 days for two reasons:

  • An index can hold up to 30 days of documents before JAVV starts a new index.
  • JAVV deletes an index only when its newest document is older than the retention.

The scanner chart runs each scanner every 6 hours by default. That is 4 cycles each day.

Example: 500 images, 40 findings for each image, two scanners, 4 cycles each day and the default retention of 90 days:

  • 500 × 40 × 2 × 4 = 160,000 documents each day.
  • 160,000 × 120 days × 280 bytes ≈ 5.4 GB.

OpenSearch also keeps each scheduled export until the export expires. The expiry time is JAVV_EXPORT_TTL_HOURS (24 hours by default). The maximum size of one export is JAVV_EXPORT_MAX_BYTES (500 MiB).

items.title: Check the shard count
items.text:
Shards are usually the first limit.

  • Each index has one primary shard.
  • Each cluster that you scan has five series of indices.
  • JAVV starts a new index in a series at the first of these limits: 30 days, 5 million documents or 50 GB.
  • JAVV deletes an index when all of its data is older than the retention of the cluster.
  • With the default settings (a new index each 30 days, a retention of 90 days), each series keeps about five indices. Thus each cluster that you scan uses about 25 shards.
  • Other indices use about 15 shards. This number does not change when you add clusters.
  • The audit log is not in that count. It starts a new index each 30 days, and JAVV never deletes it.

By default, OpenSearch permits 1,000 shards on each node (cluster.max_shards_per_node):

  • With the default settings, one node has space for about 38 clusters that you scan.
  • This number is a calculation from the default settings. Nobody did a load test to get it.
  • Each shard also uses heap memory, whatever its size.

To see the current shard count, do one of these steps:

  • In JAVV, go to Settings › Data & OpenSearch. The runtime card shows the active shards.
  • Send GET _cluster/health to OpenSearch, and read active_shards.

items.title: Make space for more shards
items.text:
Do these steps in this sequence. Stop when the shard count is low enough.

  1. Decrease the retention of the clusters that do not need a long history. Go to Settings › Data & OpenSearch › Retention, and set the retention for each cluster. A shorter retention also decreases how far time travel can go back.
  2. Increase the time between new indices in the same panel. This gives fewer, larger indices. JAVV still starts a new index at 5 million documents or at 50 GB.
  3. Delete the clusters that stopped sending scans. JAVV retires these clusters. A retired cluster uses shards until you delete it in Settings › Cluster.
  4. Add nodes. For this, use an OpenSearch that you operate (see Beyond one node). Alternatively, increase cluster.max_shards_per_node, and increase the heap by the same proportion.

items.title: Memory
items.text:
The default heap is 1 GB:

  • The compose file sets it in OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS.
  • The javv-opensearch chart sets it in opensearchJavaOpts.
  • Measured: 4 clusters, 1.7 million documents and 42 shards used about half of the heap.

Increase the heap in these two conditions:

  • The heap use stays high.
  • The OpenSearch log shows circuit_breaking_exception. This message tells you that OpenSearch refuses work to protect its memory.

Follow these rules when you increase the heap:

  • Give the OpenSearch container about two times the heap as memory. OpenSearch also uses memory outside the heap.
  • Keep the heap less than 32 GB.
  • In compose, set OPENSEARCH_JAVA_OPTS, for example -Xms2g -Xmx2g.
  • With the chart, set opensearchJavaOpts and the memory resources of the pod together.

items.title: Disk
items.text:
At 95 % disk use, OpenSearch makes the indices read-only. This limit is the flood-stage watermark of OpenSearch. When it occurs:

  • Writes fail.
  • JAVV sends 503 in reply to each scanner push. JAVV records the refused write as storage_error.
  • The scanners try the push again, with a longer wait each time. When all tries fail, a scanner keeps the push in its dead-letter file. In its next cycle, it scans the image again.
  • In the web app, reads work. Sign-in and each change fail with The store is read-only: its disk is full, and a banner on each screen says so.
  • OpenSearch keeps all the data that it stored before. New scans wait until there is disk space.
  • When there is disk space again, OpenSearch lifts the block itself. JAVV needs no restart.

To prevent this condition:

  • Keep the disk use less than about 80 %. Then a large number of scans cannot get to the limit.
  • Remember that snapshots are on the data volume. In the compose file and in the chart, path.repo is /usr/share/opensearch/data/snapshots. Thus snapshots use the same disk. Delete old snapshots, or use a snapshot repository on different storage.
  • Decrease the retention to make disk space. The lifecycle job deletes whole indices at its next run. It runs at 03:00 by default (JAVV_JOB_LIFECYCLE_SWEEP_CRON).

items.title: Beyond one node
items.text:
The compose file and the javv-opensearch chart run one OpenSearch node. The chart refuses all other values.

For more capacity, or for OpenSearch data that stays available when a node fails:

  • Operate your own OpenSearch with more nodes and with replica shards, and connect JAVV to it. See Deploying: an OpenSearch of your own.
  • JAVV needs no change for this.
  • Scaling and failures tells you which parts of JAVV scale.

items.title: Use JAVV
items.text:
These pages show how to triage the findings in JAVV, from the first scan to a finding with a decision. Each page in the table has a short video. The same steps are in text below each video.

Video What it shows From a scan to a finding How the results of the two scanners get to JAVV, and how to find one finding Set the state of a finding How to set the state of one finding, and where JAVV records the change Accept a risk, with an expiry date How to accept the risk of one CVE in a scope, and how to stop it Change many findings at once How to change the state of all the findings that match your filters When a scanner stops sending results What JAVV does when a scanner is silent for too long See who changed what How to find the changes in the Audit log and on a finding

The videos use made-up clusters and data.

Build a dashboard shows how to put panels on one page and share them.

items.title: What your role lets you do
items.text:
Your role sets what you can change:

  • To set the state of a finding, or of many findings at once, your role must allow triage. The triager, security_lead and admin roles allow it.
  • To accept a risk, or to revoke a risk acceptance, your role must allow risk acceptance. The security_lead and admin roles allow it.
  • To download a file of the data, for example a CSV or VEX file, your role must allow export. The triager, security_lead and admin roles allow it. The viewer role does not. For a viewer, each export button is not available, and the text next to it tells you why.
  • To make a dashboard, or to import one, your role must allow dashboards. The triager, security_lead and admin roles allow it. Only the owner of a dashboard or an admin can change it or remove it.

An administrator sets the role of each user.

items.title: More help
items.text: The Guide in the side menu of JAVV explains the states, the reasons and the risk acceptances.

items.title: Accept a risk, with an expiry date
items.text: A risk acceptance applies to one CVE in a scope. It also covers the new findings of that CVE in the scope.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text: • A role that allows risk acceptance: security_lead or admin (What your role lets you do).

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Open a finding from the Findings table.
  2. Select Risk-accept this CVE.
  3. Select a namespace. The acceptance covers this CVE in that namespace. A line in the dialog shows the scope.
  4. Set an expiry date. The first date that you can select is tomorrow in UTC. When this date passes, the findings become Open again.
  5. Write the reason. Other users read it on the Approval list.
  6. Select Create decision. The risk acceptance is in effect. It shows in Decisions on this CVE.
  7. The Approval list shows all the risk acceptances in effect. Open it from the side menu. Each row shows the CVE, the scope, the reason and the expiry date.

items.title: Stop a risk acceptance
items.text:
1. On the Approval list, select Revoke.
  2. Select Confirm revoke. The risk acceptance stops, and its findings become Open again.

Next: Change many findings at once.

items.title: Build a dashboard
items.text: A dashboard puts panels of Overview, Contributors and Scanner status on one page. Each panel shows the data of the cluster that you select at the top of the page.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text: • A role that allows dashboards: triager, security_lead or admin (What your role lets you do).

items.title: Make a dashboard
items.text:
1. Open Dashboards from the side menu.
  2. Select New dashboard.
  3. Type a name. The description is optional.
  4. Select who can see the dashboard: Only me, Everyone or Some roles. With Some roles, select one role or more.
  5. Select the scanner that the dashboard opens with.
  6. Select Create. The dashboard opens in edit mode, with no panels.

items.title: Add and move panels
items.text:
1. Select Add panel. The catalog shows the panels in groups.
  2. Select a panel. The preview shows the panel with the data of the selected cluster.
  3. Set the width of the panel. Some panels also have a height or a scanner to set.
  4. Select Add panel. The panel goes under the other panels.
  5. To move a panel, drag its Move tab with the mouse. A dashed box shows where the panel goes. You cannot move a panel with the keyboard.
  6. To change a panel, select Settings on the panel. To remove a panel, select the bin icon on it.
  7. Select Save changes. Discard puts back the dashboard as it was at the last save.

A dashboard has at most 24 panels.

items.title: Change the name or the sharing
items.text:
1. Open the dashboard, then select Edit dashboard.
  2. Select Name and sharing. Change the fields, then select Apply.
  3. Select Save changes.

Only the owner of a dashboard and an admin can change it. An admin can see each dashboard.

items.title: Remove a dashboard
items.text:
1. Open the dashboard, then select Edit dashboard.
  2. Select Remove, then select Remove dashboard. The data of the panels stays. The audit log keeps a copy of the dashboard.

items.title: Copy dashboards to a different JAVV
items.text:
1. On the Dashboards page, select Export all. On the page of one dashboard, select Export.
  2. On the other JAVV, open Dashboards and select Import. Select the file.
  3. Select Keep the IDs, or Make copies. You are the owner of each dashboard that the import makes.

If a dashboard in the file names a role that the other JAVV does not have, the import does not make that dashboard. The result of the import shows the line.

items.title: Change many findings at once
items.text: Bulk triage changes many findings at once. First, filter the findings.

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text: • A role that allows triage: triager, security_lead or admin (What your role lets you do).

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Select a value in a filter, for example Low in the Severity filter. The count shows how many findings match the filter.
  2. Select Bulk triage. The dialog shows your filters and the number of findings that will change.
  3. Select the new state, for example Acknowledge.
  4. Write a note. JAVV adds the note to each finding.
  5. Select Apply to matching findings. JAVV changes all the matching findings. The Audit log records one entry for the change.
  6. The State filter now counts the changed findings.

items.title: Filters that block bulk triage
items.text:
Bulk triage follows only the Severity, State and Assignee filters. Other filters, for example the Scanner filter, block it. Thus bulk triage never changes more findings than you see.

Next: When a scanner stops sending results.

items.title: How the results get to JAVV
items.text: Trivy and Grype run in your cluster. They scan each running image. Each scanner sends its results to JAVV. JAVV keeps the results of each scanner separate. It never merges them.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. All clusters shows each cluster that sends results to JAVV. Select a cluster to open it.
  2. Open Findings from the side menu. Each row is one finding: one CVE, in one package, in one image, from one scanner.
  3. To see the findings of one scanner, use the Scanner filter.
  4. Select a finding to open it. The evidence shows the result of each scanner, side by side.
  5. Set the state of the finding in the triage panel. The next page shows how.

Next: Set the state of a finding.

items.title: Set the state of a finding
path: Set the state of a finding

items.title: Prerequisites
items.text: • A role that allows triage: triager, security_lead or admin (What your role lets you do).
path: Set the state of a finding

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. Open a finding from the Findings table. The triage panel sets the state of this one finding.
  2. Select Not affected. Not affected needs a reason: select one of the five standard reasons.
  3. Select Save to audit trail. The state changes immediately.
  4. Only this finding changes. The finding of the other scanner stays Open.
  5. The Activity card of the finding shows who changed the state and when.
  6. To see all the triage changes, open the Audit log from the side menu. The new entry is at the top: when, who, and what changed.

items.title: When a scanner stops sending results
What JAVV does
items.text: Each scan refreshes the findings that the scanner sees. If a scanner sends no results for too long, JAVV marks its findings Stale. JAVV keeps the old state. When a scan sees the finding again, JAVV restores the old state.

items.title: Steps
items.text:
1. A banner on Findings shows that a scanner is silent. The data of the cluster can be old.
  2. The State filter counts the Stale findings.
  3. Open Scanner status from the side menu. It shows when each scanner sent its last results.
  4. Go back to Findings and open a Stale finding. A note shows that JAVV set this state, because the scanner is silent. A state that a person sets replaces it.

Next: See who changed what.

items.title: The Audit log
items.text:
1. Open the Audit log from the side menu. It lists each change: when, who, what and the target. A settings change shows the old and the new value of each setting that changed.
  2. To see the changes of one person, filter by user. To see the changes of a team, select more than one user.
  3. To see one type of change, filter by action, for example Bulk triage. One bulk change is one entry in the Audit log. You can select more than one action, for example Acknowledged and Resolved.
  4. To save the entries as a file, select Export CSV. Your role must allow export. If it does not, the button is not available, and the text next to it tells you why.

items.title: The history of one finding
items.text:
1. Open Findings, and open a finding.
  2. The Activity card shows each change on this one finding, with who and when. A bulk change that included this finding also shows, with the state and the note that it set.

For more help, open the Guide from the side menu of JAVV.
